This is a working paper entry from IDEAS/RePEc titled "Asymmetry in first-price auctions with affiliated private values" by Campo, S., Perrigne, I., and Vuong, Q.H. (2000), published as Economics Working Paper Archive (Toulouse) 13 by the French Institute for Agronomy Research (INRA), Economics Laboratory in Toulouse.

**Main Topic:** The paper addresses the challenge of modeling and estimating asymmetric first-price auctions within the affiliated private value (APV) paradigm, where asymmetry arises from cartels, collusion, or heterogeneity across firms.

**Key Contributions:**
- Considers two types of bidders and derives the differential equations characterizing Bayesian Nash equilibrium strategies.
- Shows these differential equations can be rewritten using the distribution of observed bids.
- Establishes identification of the asymmetric APV model and characterizes its theoretical restrictions.
- Proposes an indirect two-step nonparametric estimation procedure for estimating private value distributions by type from observed bids.
- The method does not require solving the differential equations for equilibrium strategies and can be generalized to many types of bidders.
- Provides an empirical analysis of joint bidding as an illustration.

**JEL Classification:** C14 (Semiparametric and Nonparametric Methods: General), D44 (Auctions)

**NEP Field:** NEP-AGR-2001-10-22 (Agricultural Economics)

**Note:** The full text is not available for download from this source. The item's handle is RePEc:rea:inrawp:13.

Este trabajo contiene una revisión de la literatura relevante para realizar econometría de subastas desde la perspectiva del enfoque estructural. El enfoque estructural es un marco para analizar datos de subastas en el cual la teoría y la econometría están estrechamente vinculadas. Hay tres aspectos fundamentales para el enfoque estructural: (i) Existen restricciones testeables impuestas desde el modelo teórico sobre los datos? (ii) Es posible identificar a los elementos estructurales que caracterizan una subasta sin tener que recurrir a información paramétrica a priori? (iii) Que puede decirse sobre procedimientos implementables de estimación que no se basen en supuestos paramétricos? Esta recopilación muestra como la literatura sobre el enfoque estructural ha respondido a cada una de estas preguntas. Clasificación JEL: C14, C70, D44, L10, L41 Palabras Clave: Subastas, Enfoque Estructural, Colusión, Estimación No Paramétrica, Polinomios Locales. ABSTRACT The analysis of auctions is an active area of research for both theoretical and empirical economists. This paper provides an overview of the literature relevant to the econometrics of auctions from a structural approach perspective. The structural approach is a framework to analyze auction data in which theory and econometrics are closely related. There are three fundamental issues at the heart of the structural analysis: (i) Are there any testable restrictions imposed by the theoretic model on the data? (ii) Is it possible to identify the structural elements that characterize an auction without a priori parametric information? (iii) What can be said about feasible estimation procedures which do not rely on parametric assumptions?. This survey shows how the structural approach literature has answered each question. Introduction The analysis of auctions is an active area of research for both theoretical and empirical economists. This survey attempts to summarize the state of the literature in Auction Theory as well as the Econometric Methods mainly used to estimate the theoretical models. In particular, since most of the data sets available for empirical research come from first-price auctions mechanisms, I mainly concentrate in this auction type. Auctions and procurements are widely used mechanisms to allocate public contracts, financial assets, agricultural products, natural resources, artwork and electricity, to name a few. Also, auctions throughout the internet has become quite relevant in the last few years. Given the extensive use of auctions to allocate goods and services which are frequently public, many data sets are available for empirical research. Auctions have well defined rules that can be used to build a transparent economic model. The Bayesian Nash Equilibrium (BNE) concept allows to model auctions as a game in which a buyer/seller faces a limited number of participants that behave strategically. Auctions are typically modeled as games of incomplete information in which the asymmetry of information between the buyer/seller and the participants and among the participants themselves play a key role. Until recently, the empirical analysis of auction data was limited to test some predictions from the underlying game theoretical models (see Porter (1995) for an exhaustive survey on the Reduced Form Approach). This kind of analysis is known in the literature as the Reduced Form Approach. This approach has the drawback that does not allow to do policy evaluation that would require knowledge of the informational structure of the game, like the * I am grateful to Joris Pinkse for very insightful comments and guidance. * CONICET – UNCUYO. E-Mail: orgabrielli@gmail.com. Address: Pizzurno 165 Godoy Cruz-Mendoza, Argentina. On the other hand, the Structural Approach allows the researcher to do policy evaluation by assuming that observed bids are the equilibrium bids from some auction model. Specifically, , where denotes the (observed) bid made by player i, is the equilibrium strategy and is the (unobserved) private value that player i has for the auctioned item. It is assumed that private information of the players comes from some distribution, which is common knowledge for all participants. This distribution and the individual preferences are the key elements that explain the behavior, which are the structure of the model. In other words these are the structural elements from the econometric model induced by observed bids. The Structural Approach then exploits the equilibrium relation to recover private information from participants, which then can be used to make policy recommendations. As recognized by Guerre, Perrigne and Vuong (2000) an important difficulty associated to the Structural Approach is its numerical complexity and in the implicit form of the equilibrium strategy. There are three aspects that have to be taken into account. In the first place there is an Identification issue, that is if the structure of the auction can be recovered univocally from observable variables (bids) minimizing parametric restrictions. In other words, identification implies establishing if the corresponding models can be discriminated from observable variables. A second important issue is model validity that is if the theoretical model imposes testable restrictions on the data. This working paper (Documento de Trabajo N°252, June 2023) by María Florencia Gabrielli (Universidad del Desarrollo, CONICET-UNCUYO) provides a comprehensive survey of the econometrics of first-price auctions from a structural approach perspective. The paper reviews the literature on how theory and econometrics are closely linked in auction analysis, focusing on three fundamental issues: (1) testable restrictions imposed by theoretical models on data, (2) identification of structural elements without a priori parametric information, and (3) feasible estimation procedures that do not rely on parametric assumptions.

**Key Theoretical Framework:**
The paper presents a unified view of game-theoretical models of first-price auctions, covering the Affiliated Value (AV) model and its subcategories: Independent Private Value (IPV), Affiliated Private Value (APV), and Common Value (CV) models, in both symmetric and asymmetric settings.

**Identification Results:**
- Any symmetric AV model is observationally equivalent to some symmetric APV model (unidentified in general)
- Symmetric APV and IPV models are identified
- Symmetric CV models are generally unidentified
- Asymmetric IPV and CV models are identified but can be observationally equivalent to each other
- Asymmetric CV models need not be distinguishable from symmetric ones

**Econometric Methods:**
The paper distinguishes between direct methods (parametric, ML-based, requiring computation of equilibrium strategy) and indirect methods (nonparametric, introduced by Guerre, Perrigne, and Vuong (2000)). The indirect approach is particularly advantageous as it expresses each private value as a function of the corresponding bid, the distribution of observed bids, and its density using the first-order condition, avoiding the need to solve the equilibrium strategy explicitly.

**Estimation Techniques:**
Detailed coverage of nonparametric estimators including kernel density estimators and local polynomial fitting (LPF), with discussion of bias, variance, optimal convergence rates, and bandwidth selection. LPF is noted for its superior boundary behavior compared to kernel methods.

**Collusion Analysis:**
The paper reviews collusive behavior in auctions, noting that although first-price auctions are relatively less susceptible to collusion than second-price formats, bid rigging is pervasive in markets such as public construction, school milk supply, and municipal bonds. Theoretical work by McAfee and McMillan (1992), Marshall et al. (1994), and others is discussed, along with the limited empirical literature on bidder collusion detection.

The paper concludes that the structural approach allows for policy evaluation, including optimal reserve price setting and auction mechanism design, by recovering private information from participants through equilibrium relationships.

## Abstract

We present an approach to nonparametric estimation of pseudo-values in asymmetric affiliated private values (APV) models for first price auctions that eliminates the ‘curse of dimensionality.’ We show that pseudo-values can be estimated by using two-dimensional functions of bids for APV models regardless of the form of asymmetry.

## Introduction

Structural econometrics analysis of auctions treats observed bid data as the Bayesian–Nash equilibrium of a game-theoretic auction model. An important breakthrough in the structural econometrics of first price auctions was Guerre et al. (2000)'s (GPV in the sequel) procedure that uses the equilibrium strategies to express a bidder's unobserved valuation in terms of his bid and the distribution and density functions of observed bids (see Perrigne and Vuong (1999) for a survey of recent contributions to the structural econometrics of first price auctions). GPV procedure is a two-step estimation procedure. In the first step, a sample of pseudo-values is constructed using the equilibrium inverse bid function. In the second step, the sample of pseudo-values is used to estimate the underlying density of bidders' valuations.

More recently, Campo et al. (2003) applied the same method to estimate asymmetric affiliated private values (APV) model of first price auctions. Campo et al.'s approach requires estimation of high dimensional functions of bids to construct the pseudo-values. As is well-known sample sizes required by the kernel methods to achieve a given quality of estimation (e.g., mean-square error) increase dramatically as the dimensionality of the function to be estimated increases 1. Moreover, as the number of bidder segments increases, the computational complexity of functions to be estimated increases considerably.

In this paper, we show that one only needs to estimate two-dimensional functions of bids to generate a sample of pseudo-values for the APV models regardless of the form of asymmetry. The proposed approach reduces the sample size requirements considerably and it is much simpler computationally.

args.summary:
This is a 2005 academic paper published in Economics Letters (Volume 88, Issue 3, pages 318-322) by Bin Zhang and Kemal Guler, presenting a simplified approach to nonparametric estimation of asymmetric first-price auctions. The paper addresses the "curse of dimensionality" problem in estimating pseudo-values for asymmetric affiliated private values (APV) models in first-price auctions. 

The authors build on the groundbreaking work of Guerre, Perrigne, and Vuong (GPV, 2000), which established a two-step procedure for structural econometric analysis of auctions: first constructing pseudo-values using the equilibrium inverse bid function, then estimating the underlying density of bidders' valuations. Campo et al. (2003) extended this to asymmetric APV models but required estimation of high-dimensional functions of bids, which suffers from dramatically increasing sample size requirements as dimensionality grows.

The key contribution of Zhang and Guler's approach is showing that pseudo-values can be estimated using only two-dimensional functions of bids for APV models, regardless of the form of asymmetry or the number of bidder segments. This is achieved by working with each bidder's payoff function expressed in terms of the equilibrium distribution of rival bids conditioned on the bidder's valuation. This simplification reduces sample size requirements considerably and is computationally much simpler than previous approaches.

The paper has been cited by 2 subsequent works, including a 2013 study on small business set-asides in procurement auctions published in the Journal of Public Economics, and a 2023 study on productivity in procurement auctions of pavement contracts in Mexico published in the Journal of Productivity Analysis.

URL: https://capcp.la.psu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/numericalanalysis.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This academic paper (Marshall et al., 1994, Games and Economic Behavior) presents numerical algorithms for solving first-price auction problems where bidders draw independent valuations from heterogeneous (asymmetric) distributions. The heterogeneity analyzed stems from collusion among subsets of bidders.

**Key contributions:**

1. **Problem Context:** Bidders form coalitions that create distributional asymmetries. Two scenarios are examined: (a) two coalitions facing each other, and (b) one coalition facing individual noncooperative bidders.

2. **Numerical Methodology:** The authors develop backward Taylor series expansion algorithms to solve the systems of differential equations characterizing equilibrium bid functions. These are necessary because standard forward methods fail due to pathologies at the origin (nuisance linear solutions acting as attractors). The transformed system (using auxiliary functions δ) proves numerically more stable. Convergence is achieved with N=10,000 subintervals, p=5 order expansions, and error tolerance ε of 10^-5 to 10^-8, requiring about 5 seconds of computation time on a DEC 3100 or 486/33 PC.

3. **Key Results:** 
   - For n=5 bidders, the first-price auction yields higher expected revenue for the seller than the second-price (English) auction when bidder asymmetry arises from collusion.
   - The more optimistic party (larger coalition) shades their bid more.
   - For k1=100, k2=1 (coalition vs individual), the first-price auction generates expected revenue of 0.6578 vs the second-price's 0.4999.
   - Large coalitions (e.g., k1=100) create external benefits for noncolluding bidders at first-price auctions, potentially making large all-inclusive coalitions infeasible.

4. **Theoretical Connections:** The asymmetric distribution problem is equivalent to a first-price auction between bidders with differing degrees of risk aversion. The results are consistent with existence/uniqueness proofs by Lebrun (1991) and Maskin and Riley (1991, 1992).

5. **Implications:** The paper suggests first-price auctions are less susceptible to collusion than second-price auctions, and that small all-inclusive coalitions may be feasible at first-price auctions while large ones may not be. The numerical approach enables investigation of analytically intractable problems and can be extended to more general asymmetric auctions with non-uniform distributions.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This academic paper by Bernard Lebrun (2004, York University) proves the uniqueness of the Bayesian Nash equilibrium in first-price auctions under the asymmetric independent private values model. The key condition for uniqueness is that the valuation cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) are strictly log-concave at the highest lower extremity of their supports.

The paper addresses the complexity that arises when bidders' valuations are not identically distributed. While existence results existed, uniqueness was not generally established. The author proves uniqueness under three conditions: (i) the reserve price r exceeds the highest lower support extremity c1, (ii) c1 > c2 (the second highest lower extremity), or (iii) the CDFs are strictly log-concave near (c1, c1+δ).

The proof uses a simple geometric "sliding" argument: sliding a solution of the differential equation system down the 45-degree line. This is first applied to the common-support case (Section 4), then extended to different lower extremities (Section 5.1), and finally to different upper extremities (Section 5.2). The paper relies on previous results from Lebrun (1999a) for characterization of equilibria, including the differential equation system (1) and boundary conditions.

Key implications: Uniqueness saves researchers from searching for multiple equilibria once one is found, provides robustness to numerical simulations, and is useful for experimental researchers comparing subject behavior to a single equilibrium. The log-concavity condition is weaker than requiring mass points or strictly positive continuous extensions of density functions, and many standard parametric distributions satisfy it.
</summary>

This paper by René Kirkegaard (Brock University, 2006) proposes a new approach to analyzing asymmetric first-price auctions by focusing on winning probabilities rather than directly examining bidding strategies. The key insight is that winning probabilities can be analyzed using mechanism design principles, specifically the Envelope Theorem, to derive expected payoffs and infer bidding strategies.

**Key Contributions:**

1. **Methodology**: The paper shows that analyzing winning probabilities (qi(v)) is simpler than solving the system of differential equations that characterize equilibrium bidding strategies. 2. **Strong vs. Weak Buyers (First-Order Stochastic Dominance)**: The analysis confirms that strong buyers (those with first-order stochastic dominance) are consistently better off than weak buyers for all valuations. However, no buyer wins consistently more often than another. The strong buyer's winning probability is a mean-preserving spread over the weak buyer's winning probability. The paper provides new, simpler proofs of existing results (e.g., weak buyers bid more aggressively than strong buyers under reverse hazard rate dominance).

3. **Predictable vs. Unpredictable Buyers (Second-Order Stochastic Dominance)**: This is a novel type of asymmetry not previously studied. When one buyer's valuation is more "predictable" (lower variance) than another's, the paper shows that the unpredictable buyer submits more extreme bids. <summary>
This paper presents a powerful, fully automated, and numerically robust algorithm for computing equilibrium bid functions in asymmetric, Independent Private Values (IPV), First-Price auctions. The algorithm addresses the key challenge that asymmetry prevents analytical derivation of bid functions, making numerical solutions essential.

**Key Features:**
- Solves a system of ODEs characterizing first-order conditions for Nash equilibrium using local Taylor-series expansions (piecewise polynomial approximations)
- Accommodates arbitrary numbers of bidder types, non-inclusive coalitions, and reserve prices
- Supports common distributions (Weibull, beta, normal, lognormal) with automated Taylor-series expansion generation for user-supplied distributions
- Computes inverse bid functions, probabilities of winning, expected revenues, optimal reserve prices, and probability of retention
- Includes both forward and backward extrapolation methods (with backward extrapolation from the endpoint t* to handle ill-behaved ODEs at the lower boundary)

**Methodology:**
The algorithm relies on a built-in algebra of local Taylor-series expansions. It solves the differential equations backward from the right boundary (t*), using recursive coefficient computation. The endpoint t* is found via numerical search (simplex method). The algorithm also includes automated B-spline interpolation for distributions without analytical inverse CDF expansions.

**Key Contributions:**
1. Generalizes the MMRS algorithm to arbitrary distributions without requiring stochastic dominance
2. Provides user-friendly, fully-automated implementation (FORTRAN-90)
3. Includes operational univariate quadratures for computing expected revenues and probabilities
4. Supports both auctions and procurements (first-price and second-price)
5. Offers pointwise best-response verification to check numerical accuracy

**Numerical Accuracy:**
Accuracy depends on grid fineness (500-10,000 points) and Taylor-series order (2-5). The study shows that a relatively small number of grid points (500) and low-order expansions provide nearly the same accuracy as larger configurations, with significant time savings. Computational time increases linearly with grid points and Taylor order.

**Examples Presented:**
1. Three individual bidders (low, high, median types) with Weibull distributions
2. Two bidders with crossing hazard functions (Weibull shape parameters 1.5 and 0.5)
3. Non-inclusive cartels with high-type bidders colluding against low-type bidders (lognormal distributions)

**Key Findings from Examples:**
- Asymmetric bid functions can cross when stochastic dominance does not apply
- Non-inclusive cartels can be incentive compatible in asymmetric environments, particularly when high-type bidders collude to protect informational advantages
- The algorithm includes a best-response verification method that confirmed an unusual "blip" in a coalition's bid function was a genuine equilibrium response, not a numerical error

**Procurement Version:**
The algorithm is adapted for procurements with minor modifications to the ODEs (sign changes and forward iteration instead of backward).

**Conclusion:**
The algorithm provides an unparalleled tool for numerical investigation of theoretical conjectures and empirical implementation, filling a gap in existing software (BIDCOMP2, Bajari's methods) by offering greater distributional flexibility and automated numerical stability.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This academic paper ("Auctions with Unique Equilibria" by Chawla and Hartline, EC'13) studies Bayes-Nash equilibria (BNE) in anonymous order-based auctions, particularly the generalized first-price auction (GFP) for sponsored search positions. The authors prove that when bidders' values are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) from a continuous bounded-support distribution, there is a unique Bayes-Nash equilibrium, which is symmetric and efficient. This contrasts with the generalized second-price auction (GSP), which may have no efficient equilibrium.

The approach uses two utility formulas: (1) from auction rules (allocation probability × value minus expected payment), and (2) from Myerson's characterization (utility equals integral of equilibrium winning probability). The proof shows that if strategies crossed at two distinct points, utility differences would be both equal and distinct—a contradiction.

**Key Results:**
- For two-agent symmetric auctions with rank-and-bid-based allocation, bid-based payment, and i.i.d. continuous bounded-support distributions, agents play identical strategies (except measure zero).

- For win-vs-tie-strict rank-based allocation rules (including position auctions), there is only one symmetric BNE (Theorem 4.5).
- Results extend to risk-averse agents with constant absolute risk aversion (CARA) preferences (Theorem 5.1).

**Implications:** GFP may have advantages over GSP because GFP has a unique efficient equilibrium while GSP may have no efficient equilibrium. GFP implements the same outcome as VCG without requiring knowledge of click-through rates. The price of anarchy for GFP with identical distributions is 1 (optimal), compared to the best known bound of 2.927 for GSP.
</summary>

2. **Equilibrium Characterization**: The paper characterizes two types of equilibria:

URL: https://brocku.ca/repec/pdf/0504.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper by René Kirkegaard (Brock University, 2006) proposes a new approach to analyzing asymmetric first-price auctions by focusing on winning probabilities rather than directly examining bidding strategies. The key insight is that winning probabilities can be analyzed using mechanism design principles, specifically the Envelope Theorem, to derive expected payoffs and infer bidding strategies.

**Key Contributions:**

1. **Methodology**: The paper shows that analyzing winning probabilities (qi(v)) is simpler than solving the system of differential equations that characterize equilibrium bidding strategies. The link between winning probabilities and payoffs allows the author to derive bidding strategies indirectly.

2. **Strong vs. Weak Buyers (First-Order Stochastic Dominance)**: The analysis confirms that strong buyers (those with first-order stochastic dominance) are consistently better off than weak buyers for all valuations. However, no buyer wins consistently more often than another. The strong buyer's winning probability is a mean-preserving spread over the weak buyer's winning probability. The paper provides new, simpler proofs of existing results (e.g., weak buyers bid more aggressively than strong buyers under reverse hazard rate dominance).

3. **Predictable vs. Unpredictable Buyers (Second-Order Stochastic Dominance)**: This is a novel type of asymmetry not previously studied. When one buyer's valuation is more "predictable" (lower variance) than another's, the paper shows that the unpredictable buyer submits more extreme bids. The auction format dramatically affects which buyer is better off, unlike in second-price auctions where the predictable buyer always fares better.

4. **All-Pay Auctions**: The approach extends to all-pay auctions (where all buyers pay their bid regardless of winning). The paper shows that all-pay auctions share many features with first-price auctions when comparing strong and weak buyers, though with important exceptions. A weak buyer may bid zero for a range of valuations, effectively choosing not to participate.

**Key Results:**
- The highest bid is the same for all buyers (buyers with the highest valuation are equally well off).
- Under first-order stochastic dominance, the strong buyer's distribution of bids first-order stochastically dominates the weak buyer's distribution.
- The strong buyer prefers second-price auctions; the weak buyer prefers first-price auctions (under reverse hazard rate dominance with two buyers).
- Both buyers prefer facing a weak opponent rather than a strong one.

The paper synthesizes existing literature (referencing Lebrun, Maskin & Riley, Krishna, among others) and provides new results on previously unexamined forms of asymmetry.

URL: https://www.cirje.e.u-tokyo.ac.jp/research/workshops/micro/documents/March20.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper by Kaplan and Zamir (2007) provides analytic solutions for asymmetric first-price auctions with two buyers having valuations uniformly distributed on [v1, v1] and [v2, v2], both with and without a minimum bid m. The key contributions include:

1. The paper solves the general case of asymmetric first-price auctions with uniform distributions, extending previous work by Griesmer et al. (1967) and Plum (1992) that restricted both distributions to have the same lower bound.

2. Solutions are provided for three regimes: (a) no minimum bid (or non-binding m ≤ (v1+v2)/2), (b) binding minimum bid (m > (v1+v2)/2, m ≠ v2), and (c) the special case m = v2.

3. The equilibrium bid functions are shown to be continuous in all parameters (v1, v1, v2, v2, m), including at the boundaries between regimes.

4. Several interesting examples are presented, including the first known example where bid functions intersect (cross) despite one buyer's distribution stochastically dominating the other's (Example 1: v1=0, v2=1, m=2, v2=3, v1=4).

5. A class of linear equilibrium bid functions is characterized: b1(v)=v/2+m/2 and b2(v)=v/2+m/4, which occurs when m=(2v2+v1)/3 and v1-m=v2-v2.

6. The solution also covers the case of uniform distributions with atoms at the lower end of the interval, which occurs when the minimum bid lies within the support of a buyer's distribution.

7. The paper proves continuity as one buyer's distribution collapses to a known value (v2→v2), recovering the mixed-strategy equilibrium of Kaplan and Zamir (2000).

The mathematical approach reduces the system of differential equations from first-order conditions to a single differential equation, which is then solved analytically. The solutions change form across different parameter regions, but continuity is maintained throughout.

<summary>
This theoretical paper by Hubbard and Kirkegaard (2015) addresses a critical gap in asymmetric first-price auction theory: the analysis of auctions with more than two bidders where bidders have different type supports. The standard theoretical literature either assumes exactly two bidders or an arbitrary number of bidders with types drawn from a common support. The authors argue that real-world auctions often violate these assumptions—for example, when some bidders are "strong" (e.g., billionaires) and others are "weak" (e.g., art students), their type supports differ significantly, and equilibrium behavior changes qualitatively.

The key concept introduced is "bid bifurcation"—the phenomenon where different groups of bidders submit bids over different supports, resulting in different maximum bids. The authors establish that when bid bifurcation occurs, the dimensionality of the problem increases but can be reduced using a mechanical relationship between the maximum bids of the two groups (Proposition 1). The paper shows that as the number of bidders increases, bid bifurcation becomes more likely. Comparative statics results (Proposition 3) demonstrate that bid bifurcation is more likely when bidders become "stronger" in terms of the reverse hazard rate.

The paper's main contributions are: (1) a method to reduce the dimensionality of the bid bifurcation problem, (2) necessary and sufficient conditions for bid bifurcation in the uniform case, (3) sufficient conditions for the general model, and (4) the first robust solution algorithm that allows for bid bifurcation. The authors emphasize implications for empirical work, noting that many empirical researchers have maintained the assumption of common type supports despite evidence suggesting otherwise (e.g., Flambard and Perrigne's 2006 snow removal contracts study). The results are also relevant for policy analysis, such as evaluating bid preference programs in procurement auctions.

For all pay auctions, the contrast is even greater—value-based bidding functions always cross, but rank-based functions are clearly ordered. **Fully Comprehensive Findings**

## 1. Existence and Uniqueness of Equilibrium

### Lebrun's Results on Existence and Uniqueness

Bernard Lebrun proved the existence and uniqueness of Bayesian Nash equilibrium in asymmetric first-price auctions. In Lebrun (1999), published as "First Price Auctions in the Asymmetric N Bidder Case" (International Economic Review, volume 40, issue 1, pages 125-42), the paper analyzed first price auctions where the item is awarded to the highest bidder at the price of their bid. While previous research focused on the two-bidder or symmetric case, this paper considered the general case where valuations may have different distributions, allowing an arbitrary number of bidders and mixed strategies. Key findings from this paper include: (1) every Bayesian equilibrium is an "essentially" pure equilibrium formed by bid functions whose inverses satisfy a system of differential equations with boundary conditions; (2) existence of a Bayesian equilibrium is proven; (3) uniqueness is proven when the valuation distributions have a mass point at the lower extremity of the support; (4) when all distributions are one of two atomless distributions, assumptions for uniqueness are given; (5) inequalities between equilibrium strategies are established when stochastic dominance relations exist between valuation distributions. [5]

In Lebrun (2006), "Uniqueness of the equilibrium in first-price auctions," published in Games and Economic Behavior (Volume 55, Issue 1, pages 131-151, April 2006), the paper proved that "if the value cumulative distribution functions are strictly log-concave at the highest lower extremity of their supports, a simple geometric argument establishes the uniqueness of the equilibrium of the first-price auction in the asymmetric independent private values model." [4][6] The paper addressed the uniqueness of equilibrium in first-price auctions under the asymmetric independent private values model. The key condition for uniqueness is that the valuation cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) are strictly log-concave at the highest lower extremity of their supports. [2] The paper proved uniqueness under three conditions: (i) the reserve price r exceeds the highest lower support extremity c1, (ii) c1 > c2 (the second highest lower extremity), or (iii) the CDFs are strictly log-concave near (c1, c1+δ). [2]

The proof uses a simple geometric "sliding" argument: sliding a solution of the differential equation system down the 45-degree line. This is first applied to the common-support case (Section 4), then extended to different lower extremities (Section 5.1), and finally to different upper extremities (Section 5.2). The paper relies on previous results from Lebrun (1999a) for characterization of equilibria, including the differential equation system (1) and boundary conditions. [2]

Key implications: Uniqueness saves researchers from searching for multiple equilibria once one is found, provides robustness to numerical simulations, and is useful for experimental researchers comparing subject behavior to a single equilibrium. The log-concavity condition is weaker than requiring mass points or strictly positive continuous extensions of density functions, and many standard parametric distributions satisfy it. [2] The cumulative function Fi is strictly log-concave over (c1, c1 + δ)∩(ci, di) if and only if ln Fi is strictly concave, that is, its derivative fi/Fi — the reverse hazard rate — is strictly decreasing over this interval. [2][5]

The paper Assumptions A.1 require support intervals [ci, di] with differentiable CDFs and densities locally bounded away from zero. [2]

### Tumenjargal (2026) Weaker Assumptions for Uniqueness

A more recent paper by Enkhbayar Tumenjargal, "Uniqueness of equilibrium in asymmetric first-price auctions" (Economics Letters, Volume 263, April 2026), proves the uniqueness of equilibrium in asymmetric first-price auctions under weaker assumptions than previously established. [3] The paper proves that the asymmetric independent private values first-price auction has a unique Bayesian Nash equilibrium, requiring only that valuation distributions have common support with continuously differentiable, strictly positive densities. Unlike Maskin and Riley (2003), the proof does not require mass points at the lower end of the support. Unlike Lebrun (2006), it does not require log-concavity of the distributions. [3]

The proof introduces a "shifting argument" that avoids divergence difficulties at the lower boundary in the atomless case. The result extends to single-crossing (non-risk-neutral) preferences. The model considers a first-price sealed-bid auction with n ≥ 2 risk-neutral bidders and independent private values, with reserve price r = 0 and fair tie-breaking. The paper reviews the standard argument for the mass-point case to illustrate the obstacle in the atomless case, then introduces a shifted comparison technique that sidesteps evaluation at the lower boundary entirely. The main result (Proposition 1) establishes that under Assumptions 1-2, the first-price auction has a unique Bayesian Nash equilibrium. As the paper states: "We prove that the asymmetric independent private values first-price auction has a unique Bayesian Nash equilibrium, assuming only that the valuation distributions have common support and continuously differentiable, strictly positive densities." [3]

### Maskin and Riley (2000)

The paper "Asymmetric Auctions" by Eric Maskin and John Riley (1998/2000) examines asymmetric auctions, challenging the revenue-equivalence theorem. The paper relaxes the symmetry assumption—that buyers have identical belief distributions—focusing on situations where buyers are asymmetric (one "strong," one "weak"). Three illustrative examples are presented: (1) When the strong buyer's distribution is shifted rightward, the high-bid auction generates more revenue (the "Getty effect"); (2) When the strong buyer's distribution is "stretched," the high-bid auction again yields higher revenue; (3) When probability mass is reallocated to the lower end of the weak buyer's distribution, the open auction is superior. General propositions (3.3-3.5) formalize these findings. Key results include: the strong buyer prefers the open auction while the weak buyer prefers the high-bid auction (Proposition 2.6); the high-bid auction is superior for distribution shifts and stretches; the open auction is superior for shifts of probability mass to the lower endpoint. The paper also provides numerical examples showing significant revenue differences (ranging from 6% to 48% depending on the asymmetry). [22]

### Conditions for Strictly Increasing Bid Functions and Atomless Distributions with Connected Supports

The characterization of equilibrium in asymmetric first-price auctions uses inverse bid functions satisfying a system of differential equations with boundary conditions. The equilibrium bid functions are strictly increasing when the valuation distributions are atomless with connected supports. [2][5] The requirement that the inverse hazard rate functions are well-behaved is central to the existence and uniqueness proofs. The reverse hazard rate (fi/Fi) being strictly decreasing is equivalent to strict log-concavity of the CDF, which is the key condition in Lebrun's uniqueness proof. [2][5]

Bajari (2001) demonstrated that the equilibrium to the model is unique and described three algorithms for computing inverse equilibrium bid functions. [21]

Marshall et al. (1994) noted that the asymmetric distribution problem is equivalent to a first-price auction between bidders with differing degrees of risk aversion. The results are consistent with existence/uniqueness proofs by Lebrun (1991) and Maskin and Riley (1991, 1992). [1][12]

### The Rank-Based Approach of Hopkins (2007)

Hopkins (2007) proposed a new rank-based methodology for analyzing first price and all pay auctions. Instead of writing bidding functions as functions of values, the method uses the rank or quantile of a bidder's value in the distribution from which it was drawn. This approach offers three key advantages: (1) it easily handles different supports, making bidding functions directly comparable across bidders; (2) it requires weaker conditions (simple stochastic dominance rather than reverse hazard rate dominance); and (3) it gives clearer results where standard methods yield ambiguous or crossing bid functions. In asymmetric first price auctions, if one bidder has a stochastically higher distribution of values, her bidding function in terms of rank is always higher than her rival's (the opposite of what value-based methods show, where the weaker bidder bids more for a given value). [17]

---

## 2. The "Gap" at the Top of the Bidding Functions

### Different Upper Bounds and Bunching at the Top

When one bidder's valuation distribution has a higher upper bound than the other's, the bidder with the lower upper bound's bid function flattens out at the top. This is the phenomenon of the "gap at the top" or "bunching" or "constraint" at the top. The condition is that b_max = min(β1(v1_high), β2(v2_high)), meaning the maximum bid in the auction is the minimum of the two bidders' bids at their respective highest valuations. [2][5]

Lebrun (2006) extended the uniqueness proof to cases with different upper extremities (Section 5.2). [2]

### Bid Bifurcation / Bid-Separation

Hubbard and Kirkegaard (2015) introduced the concept of "bid bifurcation"—the phenomenon where different groups of bidders submit bids over different supports, resulting in different maximum bids. The paper addresses a critical gap in asymmetric first-price auction theory: the analysis of auctions with more than two bidders where bidders have different type supports. The standard theoretical literature either assumes exactly two bidders or an arbitrary number of bidders with types drawn from a common support. The authors argue that real-world auctions often violate these assumptions—for example, when some bidders are "strong" (e.g., billionaires) and others are "weak" (e.g., art students), their type supports differ significantly, and equilibrium behavior changes qualitatively. [13]

The key concept introduced is "bid bifurcation"—the phenomenon where different groups of bidders submit bids over different supports, resulting in different maximum bids. The authors establish that when bid bifurcation occurs, the dimensionality of the problem increases but can be reduced using a mechanical relationship between the maximum bids of the two groups (Proposition 1). Specifically, the unknown pair (b̂v, bn) can be reduced to a one-dimensional problem, making the general case no more computationally complex than the standard common-support case. [13]

Using uniform distributions as a benchmark, the authors derive precise conditions for bid bifurcation (Proposition 2). For example, with three strong bidders and two weak bidders, bid bifurcation occurs if the strong bidders' highest type exceeds the weak bidders' by more than 8.11%. The paper shows that as the number of bidders increases, bid bifurcation becomes more likely. Comparative statics results (Proposition 3) demonstrate that bid bifurcation is more likely when bidders become "stronger" in terms of the reverse hazard rate. [13]

Proposition 1 states: "For any bn ∈ (b, vn), b̂v is uniquely determined by b̂v = min{v1, (m1/(m1-1))vn - (1/(m1-1))bn}." Corollary 1: "In equilibrium, bn < b1 if b > bc." Proposition 3: "Assume Gi ⪰ Fi, i = 1, n and m1, mn ≥ 2. Assume there is a binding reserve price in place, with r ∈ (v, min{v1, vn}). Then, bGn ≥ bFn and thus b̂vG ≤ b̂vF. Consequently, if bid bifurcation occurs under (F1, Fn) it also occurs under (G1, Gn); i.e., when bidders become stronger." [13]

The paper's main contributions are: (1) a method to reduce the dimensionality of the bid bifurcation problem, (2) necessary and sufficient conditions for bid bifurcation in the uniform case, (3) sufficient conditions for the general model, and (4) the first robust solution algorithm that allows for bid bifurcation. [13]

Hubbard and Kirkegaard (2019) further studied "bid-separation" in asymmetric first-price auctions with more than two bidders. The theoretical literature has mainly focused on settings with either (1) exactly two bidders or (2) an arbitrary number of bidders with types in a common support. The authors explore complications when moving beyond these settings, where bidders may tender bids over different intervals—a property termed bid-separation. [6]

Key findings include: Bid-separation is more prevalent the more bidders there are and the "stronger" bidders are on their respective supports. A critical threshold b_c = m₁v_n - (m₁-1)v₁ determines whether bid-separation occurs: if b_n > b_c, then bid-separation results. In the uniform-distribution model, explicit conditions are derived. For example, with three strong and two weak bidders, bid-separation occurs if v₁ is more than 8.11% larger than v₂. The paper shows that bid-separation invalidates existing numerical solution methods, but provides a modified approach to handle it. Bid-separation has design implications for revenue comparisons across auction formats and for analyzing bid preference policies in procurement auctions. [6]

### Kaplan and Zamir (2007) on Uniform Distributions

Kaplan and Zamir (2007) provided analytic solutions for asymmetric first-price auctions with two buyers having valuations uniformly distributed on [v1, v1] and [v2, v2], both with and without a minimum bid m. The paper solves the general case of asymmetric first-price auctions with uniform distributions, extending previous work by Griesmer et al. (1967) and Plum (1992) that restricted both distributions to have the same lower bound. Solutions are provided for three regimes: (a) no minimum bid (or non-binding m ≤ (v1+v2)/2), (b) binding minimum bid (m > (v1+v2)/2, m ≠ v2), and (c) the special case m = v2. The equilibrium bid functions are shown to be continuous in all parameters (v1, v1, v2, v2, m), including at the boundaries between regimes. Several interesting examples are presented, including the first known example where bid functions intersect (cross) despite one buyer's distribution stochastically dominating the other's (Example 1: v1=0, v2=1, m=2, v2=3, v1=4). A class of linear equilibrium bid functions is characterized: b1(v)=v/2+m/2 and b2(v)=v/2+m/4, which occurs when m=(2v2+v1)/3 and v1-m=v2-v2. The solution also covers the case of uniform distributions with atoms at the lower end of the interval, which occurs when the minimum bid lies within the support of a buyer's distribution. [13]

## 3. Numerical Methods

### The Coupled ODE System

The equilibrium in asymmetric first-price auctions is characterized by a system of differential equations for the inverse bid functions. The ODE system for inverse bid functions is given by: v′_i(b) = F_i(v_i)/f_i(v_i) * [(1/(n-1) * Σ 1/(v_j - b)) - 1/(v_i - b)]. [21] The system of differential equations characterizing first-order conditions for Nash equilibrium must be solved numerically. [1][15]

### The Shooting Method (Forward and Reverse)

#### Reverse Shooting from the Top

Marshall et al. (1994) developed backward Taylor series expansion algorithms to solve the systems of differential equations characterizing equilibrium bid functions. These are necessary because standard forward methods fail due to pathologies at the origin (nuisance linear solutions acting as attractors). The transformed system (using auxiliary functions δ) proves numerically more stable. Convergence is achieved with N=10,000 subintervals, p=5 order expansions, and error tolerance ε of 10^-5 to 10^-8, requiring about 5 seconds of computation time on a DEC 3100 or 486/33 PC. [1][12]

As Marshall et al. stated: "Our first recommendation is that systems of differential equations such as those consisting of Eqs. (2) and (3) should be solved backward starting from an assumed terminal point using the initial condition (4) as an indicator of whether or not we have used the correct value for t*." [1][12]

#### Fibich and Gavish (2011): The Boundary-Value Method

Fibich and Gavish (2011), "Numerical simulations of asymmetric first-price auctions," Games and Economic Behavior, 73, 479-495, addressed the computational challenges of determining equilibrium strategies in asymmetric first-price auctions. The authors demonstrate that the standard backward-shooting method for computing these strategies is inherently unstable, with instability worsening as the number of bidders increases. They introduce a novel boundary-value method as a robust and stable alternative, capable of handling auctions with any number of players and mixed distribution types—including distributions with multiple crossings. [7][10][12]

The key findings from Fibich and Gavish: "The standard method for computing the equilibrium strategies of asymmetric first-price auctions is the backward-shooting method. In this study we show that the backward-shooting method is inherently unstable, and that this instability cannot be eliminated by changing the numerical methodology of the backward solver. Moreover, this instability becomes more severe as the number of players increases. We then present a novel boundary-value method for computing the equilibrium strategies of asymmetric first-price auctions." [7][10]

The boundary-value method recasts the problem as a function of v_n on the fixed domain [0,1]. The method handles reserve prices by transforming the system so the left boundary does not have infinite derivatives. The boundary-value method converges linearly with fixed-point iterations (25-50 iterations) and quadratically with Newton's method. Matlab code is provided in appendices. [21]

Using this new method, the authors study large auctions with hundreds of players, compute the asymptotic rate at which large first-price and second-price auctions become revenue equivalent (the revenue difference decays as 1/n³ or even faster), and analyze auctions where distributions cannot be ordered by first-order stochastic dominance. [7][10][21]

Nir Gavish provides MATLAB codes for computing equilibrium bids in asymmetric first-price auctions on his website, implementing the boundary-value method developed with Gadi Fibich. The codes are for two players (fixed-point iterations and Newton's iterations), three players, and an enhanced version for two players that computes revenue with better accuracy. [11]

#### The Continuation Method

The continuation method is related to the boundary-value approach. The boundary-value method transforms the system of nonlinear ODEs to a fixed domain by changing the independent variable, allowing solution via standard fixed-point or Newton iterations. [21] While not explicitly called "continuation method" in the sources, the approach of solving on a transformed domain with fixed-point iterations is closely related to continuation/homotopy methods.

### The Relaxation Method

The paper by Au, Banks, and Guo (2021), "Numerical Solution of Asymmetric Auctions" (INFORMS Decision Analysis, Volume 18(4), pages 321-334), proposes the backward indifference derivation (BID) algorithm, a novel numerical method for approximating pure strategy Nash equilibrium (PSNE) bidding functions in asymmetric first-price auctions. Unlike prevailing numerical methods that rely on systems of poorly behaved differential equations, the BID algorithm constructs a sequence of finite-action PSNE that converges to the continuum-action PSNE by finding where bidders are indifferent between actions. The authors prove convergence (conditional on knowing the maximum bid) and evaluate the algorithm's numerical performance on four examples, two of which have not been previously addressed. [14][20]

### Finite Difference Methods

The Dharanan et al. paper from ISID emphasizes that specialized BVP solvers (e.g., MIRK 4) are necessary—not standard IVP solvers or shooting methods—due to stiffness and the two-point boundary nature of the ODE system. They implement simulations in Julia with three numerical examples: (1) two U[0,10] and one U[0,8] bidders; (2) two with quadratic distribution F(x)=x²/100 on [0,10] and one U[0,8]; (3) two U[0,10] and one U[2,8] bidders. [16] The paper states: "In reality, this problem is a two-point BVP. Therefore, the numerical value computed at any point x ∈ (c, η) depends upon boundary conditions at both c and η. IVP solvers do not take this fact into account and use only one boundary condition." [16]

### Hubbard and Paarsch (2009) and Hubbard, Kirkegaard, Paarsch (2013)

Hubbard and Paarsch (2009), "Investigating bid preferences at low-price, sealed-bid auctions with endogenous participation," International Journal of Industrial Organization, Volume 27, Issue 1, pages 1-14, January 2009, investigated procurement auctions with bid preference policies where qualified firms are treated specially by scaling their bids with a discount factor for evaluation purposes. The authors identify three effects of this asymmetry: (1) preferred firms may inflate their bids yet still win; (2) nonpreferred firms may bid more aggressively than in the absence of preferences; (3) the preference policy can affect participation. Using numerical solutions for equilibrium bid functions under different discounts and simulating behavior, they quantify the relative importance of these three effects. The key finding is that the participation effect is relatively unimportant, and in most cases, a positive cost-minimizing preference rate exists. [15]

Hubbard, Kirkegaard, and Paarsch (2013), "Using Economic Theory to Guide Numerical Analysis: Solving for Equilibria in Models of Asymmetric First-Price Auctions," Computational Economics, Volume 42, pages 241-266, addresses the challenge of deriving explicit equilibrium bid functions in asymmetric first-price auction models, where explicit solutions are typically impossible. The authors employ numerical methods, approximating inverse-bid functions with polynomials, and use theoretical results both to solve for polynomial coefficients and to evaluate the quality of approximations. They find that low-degree polynomial approximations perform poorly and can lead to incorrect policy recommendations regarding auction design. The paper emphasizes the need for researchers to obtain high-quality numerical solutions. As they state: "We approximate the (inverse-)bid functions by polynomials and employ theoretical results in two ways: to help solve for the polynomial coefficients and to evaluate qualitatively the appropriateness of a given approximation." [9][10][11]

The authors propose plotting bidders' relative expected pay-offs as a quick, informative way to check whether approximate solutions are consistent with theory. [13][14]

### Wang, Shen, Zuo (2020) - Discrete Distributions

Wang, Shen, and Zuo (AAMAS 2020) studied the Bayesian Nash Equilibrium (BNE) in first-price auctions where buyers' values are drawn from discrete distributions—a setting motivated by the display advertising industry's shift to first-price auctions. They provide a constructive proof of existence (Theorem 5.2) and uniqueness (Theorem 5.4) of the BNE in the discrete case, without requiring the strict log-concavity assumptions needed in continuous settings. They provide an algorithm (backward-shooting type) that computes the BNE by determining a "bidding set" that changes as the bid decreases (Algorithm 1 and 2). Unlike continuous approaches, this method does not involve solving ordinary differential equations, avoiding solution errors, oscillation problems, and sensitivity issues. Experimental results show the discrete algorithm is both faster and more accurate than continuous approximation methods—for 1000 small instances (n=5, d=5), the discrete algorithm finished 955 instances within 30 seconds (tol=10^-8), while the continuous algorithm finished only 22 instances (tol=0.01). [8]

## 4. The "Reverse Shooting" Method

The reverse shooting method (also called backward-shooting method) is the standard approach for computing equilibrium strategies in asymmetric first-price auctions. The method involves starting from the highest bid at the top of the common support and integrating backwards. [7][10][21]

Marshall et al. (1994) first recommended this approach: "Our first recommendation is that systems of differential equations such as those consisting of Eqs. (2) and (3) should be solved backward starting from an assumed terminal point using the initial condition (4) as an indicator of whether or not we have used the correct value for t*." [1][12]

The method works as follows: The algorithm relies on a built-in algebra of local Taylor-series expansions. It solves the differential equations backward from the right boundary (t*), using recursive coefficient computation. The endpoint t* is found via numerical search (simplex method). The algorithm also includes automated B-spline interpolation for distributions without analytical inverse CDF expansions. [1][15]

However, Fibich and Gavish (2011) demonstrated that the backward-shooting method is inherently unstable, and this instability cannot be eliminated by changing the numerical methodology of the backward solver. Moreover, this instability becomes more severe as the number of players increases. The instability of the backward-shooting method is not a 'technical issue', but rather an inherent analytic property of backward solutions. [7][10][21] They showed that the backward-shooting method's instability is proven analytically for symmetric auctions and shown numerically for asymmetric ones. [21]

The boundary-value method is presented as a more robust alternative to reverse shooting. In particular, unlike backward shooting, it performs well even when the number of players is large, and for mixed types of distributions. [21]

The Dharanan et al. paper also notes that the problem is a two-point BVP, so the numerical value computed at any point x ∈ (c, η) depends upon boundary conditions at both c and η. IVP solvers do not take this fact into account and use only one boundary condition. [16]

## 5. Computational Approaches: References

### Bajari (2001)

Bajari (2001), "Comparing competition and collusion: a numerical approach," Economic Theory, vol. 18, issue 1, pages 187-205, studied a model of first price sealed bid procurement auctions with asymmetric bidders. Bajari demonstrated that the equilibrium to the model is unique and described three algorithms for computing inverse equilibrium bid functions. The computational algorithms are used to compare competitive and collusive bidding, and they are useful for structural estimation of auction models and assessing damages from bid-rigging. [21]

### Gayle and Richard (2008)

Gayle and Richard (2008), "Numerical Solutions of Asymmetric, First-Price, Independent Private Values Auctions," Computational Economics, Volume 32, pages 245-278, proposed a fully automated and numerically robust algorithm for computing equilibrium bid functions in asymmetric first-price auctions with independent private values. [1][2][6]

Key aspects of the algorithm include: uses built-in algebra of local Taylor-series expansions to solve differential equations characterizing first-order conditions; user-friendly menu allowing assignment of common distributions to bidders and creation of arbitrary coalitions; computes inverse bid functions and auxiliary statistics such as expected revenues, probabilities of winning, retention probabilities under reserve pricing, and optimal reserve prices; accommodates user-supplied distributions (analytical or tabulated) with an automatic procedure for local Taylor-series expansions. The tool is designed for both theoretical investigation and empirical inference procedures. [1][2][6]

The algorithm generalizes the MMRS algorithm to arbitrary distributions without requiring stochastic dominance, provides user-friendly, fully-automated implementation (FORTRAN-90), includes operational univariate quadratures for computing expected revenues and probabilities, supports both auctions and procurements (first-price and second-price), and offers pointwise best-response verification to check numerical accuracy. [1][15]

Accuracy depends on grid fineness (500-10,000 points) and Taylor-series order (2-5). The study shows that a relatively small number of grid points (500) and low-order expansions provide nearly the same accuracy as larger configurations, with significant time savings. Computational time increases linearly with grid points and Taylor order. [1][15]

### Marshall, Meurer, Richard, and Stromquist (1994) (MMRS)

Marshall, Meurer, Richard, and Stromquist (1994), "Numerical Analysis of Asymmetric First Price Auctions," Games and Economic Behavior, presented numerical algorithms for solving first-price auction problems where bidders draw independent valuations from heterogeneous (asymmetric) distributions. The heterogeneity analyzed stems from collusion among subsets of bidders. Two scenarios are examined: (a) two coalitions facing each other, and (b) one coalition facing individual noncooperative bidders. [1][12]

The key results from MMRS include: For n=5 bidders, the first-price auction yields higher expected revenue for the seller than the second-price (English) auction when bidder asymmetry arises from collusion. The more optimistic party (larger coalition) shades their bid more. For k1=100, k2=1 (coalition vs individual), the first-price auction generates expected revenue of 0.6578 vs the second-price's 0.4999. Large coalitions (e.g., k1=100) create external benefits for noncolluding bidders at first-price auctions, potentially making large all-inclusive coalitions infeasible. [1][12]

### Kirkegaard (2006, 2009)

Kirkegaard (2006), "A Simple Approach to Analyzing Asymmetric First Price Auctions," proposed a new approach to analyzing asymmetric first-price auctions by focusing on winning probabilities rather than directly examining bidding strategies. The key insight is that winning probabilities can be analyzed using mechanism design principles, specifically the Envelope Theorem, to derive expected payoffs and infer bidding strategies. [5][11]

Key results include: The highest bid is the same for all buyers (buyers with the highest valuation are equally well off). Under first-order stochastic dominance, the strong buyer's distribution of bids first-order stochastically dominates the weak buyer's distribution. The strong buyer prefers second-price auctions; the weak buyer prefers first-price auctions (under reverse hazard rate dominance with two buyers). Both buyers prefer facing a weak opponent rather than a strong one. [5][11]

Kirkegaard (2009), "Asymmetric first price auctions," Journal of Economic Theory, Volume 144, Issue 4, pages 1617-1635, proposed a new approach to analyzing asymmetric first price auctions by examining the ratio of bidders' endogenous payoffs compared to the ratio of exogenous distribution functions describing beliefs, rather than examining bidding strategies directly. It is proven that first order stochastic dominance is necessary for bidding strategies not to cross. When this assumption is relaxed in the numerical literature, it leads to exactly one crossing, but examples with several crossings can be constructed. Bid distributions will cross in auctions with two bidders whenever second order (but not first order) stochastic dominance applies. [9]

### Hubbard, Kirkegaard, and Paarsch (2013)

Hubbard, Kirkegaard, and Paarsch (2013), "Using Economic Theory to Guide Numerical Analysis: Solving for Equilibria in Models of Asymmetric First-Price Auctions," Computational Economics, Volume 42, pages 241-266, addressed the challenge of deriving explicit equilibrium bid functions in asymmetric first-price auction models. The authors approximate inverse-bid functions using polynomials and apply theoretical results to both solve for polynomial coefficients and evaluate the quality of approximations. They find that low-degree polynomial approximations perform poorly and can lead to incorrect policy recommendations regarding auction design, emphasizing the need for quality solutions. [9][10][11]

### Au, Banks, and Guo (2021) - BID Algorithm

Au, Banks, and Guo (2021), "Numerical Solution of Asymmetric Auctions," INFORMS Decision Analysis, Volume 18(4), pages 321-334, proposed the backward indifference derivation (BID) algorithm, a new method to numerically approximate the pure strategy Nash equilibrium (PSNE) bidding functions in asymmetric first-price auctions. The BID algorithm constructs a sequence of finite-action PSNE that converges to the continuum-action PSNE by finding where bidders are indifferent between actions. The authors prove convergence (conditional on knowing the maximum bid) and evaluate the algorithm's numerical performance on four examples, two of which have not been previously addressed. [14][20]

### Dharanan et al. - Perturbation Method

The Dharanan et al. paper from ISID identifies a critical flaw in Lebrun (2006)'s characterization approach for computing Bayesian Nash Equilibria in settings with asymmetric supports: it reduces to an ill-posed Differential Algebraic Equations (DAE) problem that cannot be solved numerically. They develop a perturbation method—approximating an auction with asymmetric supports by a sequence of auctions with common support. They prove that the limit of equilibria of perturbed games is the equilibrium of the limit game (Theorem 1), and that the BNE of the perturbed game is an ε-BNE of the original auction (Theorem 4). They characterize the equilibrium as continuous and piece-wise differentiable (Theorems 2 and 3). For numerical computation, they emphasize that specialized BVP solvers (e.g., MIRK 4) are necessary—not standard IVP solvers or shooting methods—due to stiffness and the two-point boundary nature of the ODE system. They implement simulations in Julia with three numerical examples. [16]

### Gayle (2004) - Numerical Analysis with Reserve Prices

Gayle (2004), "Numerical Analysis of Asymmetric First Price Auctions with Reserve Prices," develops a numerical algorithm for solving first-price sealed-bid auction problems where bidders draw independent private values from heterogeneous distributions, groups of symmetric bidders may collude, and the auctioneer sets a reserve price. The algorithm extends the work of MMRS and allows for: (1) ex-ante heterogeneity in distributions of private values, (2) collusive coalitions, (3) non-uniform distributions (not just uniform), (4) an arbitrary number of bidder types, and (5) reserve prices. The algorithm solves the system of ordinary differential equations characterizing asymmetric Nash equilibrium by applying recursive piecewise low-order Taylor series expansions. Key transformation involves defining li(t) = Fi(λi(t)) to reduce dimensionality. The solution addresses a "two-point boundary value problem" with singularity at the origin, solved by backward recursion from an assumed terminal point. Convergence is achieved via simplex search (AMOEBA) minimizing an objective function. [10]

### Maskin and Riley (2007) - Auction Choice

Li and Riley (2007), "Auction Choice," International Journal of Industrial Organization, Volume 25, Issue 6, pages 1269-1298, developed a robust method for computing equilibrium bid functions and used numerical analysis to show that the effects of affiliation and risk aversion on revenue are typically small, while the effects of asymmetry between bidders are economically large—unless the auctioneer has as much information about bidders as they do about each other. The paper also characterizes the effects of asymmetry for the n-bidder case. [4]

This paper presents a study on Bayesian Nash Equilibrium (BNE) in first-price auctions with discrete value distributions. The authors (Zihe Wang, Weiran Shen, and Song Zuo) from Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Carnegie Mellon University, and Google Research provide an algorithm to compute the BNE, prove existence and uniqueness, and characterize the equilibrium structure.

URL: https://www.weiran-shen.info/page_files/bayesian_nash_equilibrium_in_first-price_auction_with_discrete_value_distributions.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents a study on Bayesian Nash Equilibrium (BNE) in first-price auctions with discrete value distributions. The authors (Zihe Wang, Weiran Shen, and Song Zuo) from Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Carnegie Mellon University, and Google Research provide an algorithm to compute the BNE, prove existence and uniqueness, and characterize the equilibrium structure.

**Key contributions:**
1. An efficient algorithm for computing BNE in first-price auctions under discrete value distributions that does not require solving ordinary differential equations (ODEs), making it faster and more robust than continuous methods.
2. A constructive proof of existence of BNE in the discrete case.
3. A proof of uniqueness of BNE (Theorem 5.4), without requiring the strict log-concavity assumptions needed in continuous cases.
4. Introduction of the "bidding set" concept (Definition 4.1) to analyze how the set of buyers who bid at a given price changes as the bid decreases.
5. The algorithm falls in the "backward-shooting" category—it guesses the largest winning bid and computes strategies down to the smallest winning bid, then iteratively refines the guess.

**Key theoretical results:**
- The smallest winning bid b is determined by the buyer with the largest smallest value (Lemma 2.2).
- Bidding strategies are monotone in value (Lemma 2.5).
- Each buyer's bidding set for a given value is a connected interval (Theorem 4.3).
- The position where the algorithm stops is strictly monotone and continuous in the guessed largest winning bid (Corollary 4.11, Theorem 4.12).

**Experimental results:** The discrete algorithm outperforms continuous approximation methods (e.g., Algorithm 3) in both accuracy and speed. For small instances (n=5, d=5 values), the discrete algorithm finished 955 out of 1000 instances within 30 seconds, while the continuous algorithm finished only 22 instances with tol=0.01. For medium instances (n=10, d=10), the discrete algorithm finished 512 instances while the continuous algorithm finished none.

The paper is motivated by the shift from second-price to first-price auctions in display advertising, where credibility is a major concern. The discrete value setting is justified because real-world observations are finite, and the discrete approach provides structural insights not available in continuous cases.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: Numerical Analysis of Asymmetric First Price Auctions ---
URL: https://capcp.la.psu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/numericalanalysis.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This academic paper (Marshall et al., 1994, Games and Economic Behavior) presents numerical algorithms for solving first-price auction problems where bidders draw independent valuations from heterogeneous (asymmetric) distributions. The heterogeneity analyzed stems from collusion among subsets of bidders.

**Key contributions:**

1. **Problem Context:** Bidders form coalitions that create distributional asymmetries. Two scenarios are examined: (a) two coalitions facing each other, and (b) one coalition facing individual noncooperative bidders.

2. **Numerical Methodology:** The authors develop backward Taylor series expansion algorithms to solve the systems of differential equations characterizing equilibrium bid functions. These are necessary because standard forward methods fail due to pathologies at the origin (nuisance linear solutions acting as attractors). The transformed system (using auxiliary functions δ) proves numerically more stable. Convergence is achieved with N=10,000 subintervals, p=5 order expansions, and error tolerance ε of 10^-5 to 10^-8, requiring about 5 seconds of computation time on a DEC 3100 or 486/33 PC.

3. **Key Results:** 
   - For n=5 bidders, the first-price auction yields higher expected revenue for the seller than the second-price (English) auction when bidder asymmetry arises from collusion.
   - The more optimistic party (larger coalition) shades their bid more.
   - For k1=100, k2=1 (coalition vs individual), the first-price auction generates expected revenue of 0.6578 vs the second-price's 0.4999.
   - Large coalitions (e.g., k1=100) create external benefits for noncolluding bidders at first-price auctions, potentially making large all-inclusive coalitions infeasible.

4. **Theoretical Connections:** The asymmetric distribution problem is equivalent to a first-price auction between bidders with differing degrees of risk aversion. The results are consistent with existence/uniqueness proofs by Lebrun (1991) and Maskin and Riley (1991, 1992).

5. **Implications:** The paper suggests first-price auctions are less susceptible to collusion than second-price auctions, and that small all-inclusive coalitions may be feasible at first-price auctions while large ones may not be. The numerical approach enables investigation of analytically intractable problems and can be extended to more general asymmetric auctions with non-uniform distributions.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: Multiple equilibria in asymmetric first-price auctions ---
URL: https://mpra.ub.uni-muenchen.de/34937/1/MPRA_paper_34937.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This academic paper by Todd R. Kaplan and Shmuel Zamir, published on MPRA in November 2011, challenges the established uniqueness result for Bayes-Nash equilibria in asymmetric first-price auctions. While Maskin and Riley (2003) and Lebrun (2006) proved uniqueness under the assumption that buyers never bid above their values, the authors demonstrate that relaxing this assumption can produce multiple "substantial" additional equilibria. These non-standard equilibria feature buyers who sometimes bid above their values (though never winning with such bids), and can produce different allocations of the object and different selling prices.

The paper uses a detailed example with two buyers (values uniformly drawn from [0,5] and [6,7] respectively) and no minimum bid, showing three distinct equilibria: one standard equilibrium and two non-standard equilibria, each with different revenue outcomes (3.99, 4.27, and 5 respectively) and probabilities of buyer 1 winning (0.133, 0.1, and 0).

The authors prove four key propositions: (1) any standard equilibrium can form a non-standard equilibrium with a smaller minimum bid; (2) if the minimum bid exceeds the maximum possible value, no non-standard equilibrium exists; (3) this condition can be extended to equivalence relationships; and (4) any non-standard equilibrium has an equivalent standard equilibrium with a higher minimum bid. The paper also shows that such multiplicity can only occur in asymmetric auctions—symmetric auctions have no non-standard equilibria. The authors conclude that the assumption that buyers do not bid above their values should be treated more carefully in asymmetric auction analysis.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper by Kaplan and Zamir (2007) provides analytic solutions for asymmetric first-price auctions with two buyers having valuations uniformly distributed on [v1, v1] and [v2, v2], both with and without a minimum bid m. The key contributions include:

1. The paper solves the general case of asymmetric first-price auctions with uniform distributions, extending previous work by Griesmer et al. (1967) and Plum (1992) that restricted both distributions to have the same lower bound.

--- SOURCE 13: Asymmetric Auctions with More Than Two Bidders ---
URL: https://www.uoguelph.ca/economics/repec/workingpapers/2015/2015-02.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This theoretical paper by Hubbard and Kirkegaard (2015) addresses a critical gap in asymmetric first-price auction theory: the analysis of auctions with more than two bidders where bidders have different type supports. The standard theoretical literature either assumes exactly two bidders or an arbitrary number of bidders with types drawn from a common support. The authors argue that real-world auctions often violate these assumptions—for example, when some bidders are "strong" (e.g., billionaires) and others are "weak" (e.g., art students), their type supports differ significantly, and equilibrium behavior changes qualitatively.

The key concept introduced is "bid bifurcation"—the phenomenon where different groups of bidders submit bids over different supports, resulting in different maximum bids. The authors establish that when bid bifurcation occurs, the dimensionality of the problem increases but can be reduced using a mechanical relationship between the maximum bids of the two groups (Proposition 1). Specifically, the unknown pair (b̂v, bn) can be reduced to a one-dimensional problem, making the general case no more computationally complex than the standard common-support case.

Using uniform distributions as a benchmark, the authors derive precise conditions for bid bifurcation (Proposition 2). For example, with three strong bidders and two weak bidders, bid bifurcation occurs if the strong bidders' highest type exceeds the weak bidders' by more than 8.11%. The paper shows that as the number of bidders increases, bid bifurcation becomes more likely. Comparative statics results (Proposition 3) demonstrate that bid bifurcation is more likely when bidders become "stronger" in terms of the reverse hazard rate.

The paper's main contributions are: (1) a method to reduce the dimensionality of the bid bifurcation problem, (2) necessary and sufficient conditions for bid bifurcation in the uniform case, (3) sufficient conditions for the general model, and (4) the first robust solution algorithm that allows for bid bifurcation. The authors emphasize implications for empirical work, noting that many empirical researchers have maintained the assumption of common type supports despite evidence suggesting otherwise (e.g., Flambard and Perrigne's 2006 snow removal contracts study). The results are also relevant for policy analysis, such as evaluating bid preference programs in procurement auctions.
</summary>

3. **Semiparametric Identification**: To achieve identification, the authors exploit heterogeneity across auctioned objects and impose two restrictions: (a) the utility function is parametric (e.g., CRRA or CARA), and (b) the conditional private value distribution satisfies a parametric quantile restriction (e.g., a constant α-quantile).
