<webpage_content>
ON THE CONVERGENCE OF LEARNING ALGORITHMS IN BAYESIAN AUCTION GAMES Martin Bichler Department of Computer Science Technical University of Munich bichler@cit.tum.de Stephan B. Lunowa Department of Mathematics Technical University of Munich stephan.lunowa@tum.de Matthias Oberlechner Department of Computer Science Technical University of Munich matthias.oberlechner@tum.de Fabian R. Pieroth Department of Computer Science Technical University of Munich fabian.pieroth@tum.de Barbara Wohlmuth Department of Mathematics Technical University of Munich wohlmuth@tum.de December 18, 2024 ABSTRACT Equilibrium problems in Bayesian auction games can be described as systems of differential equations.
Depending on the model assumptions, these equations might be such that we do not have a rigorous mathematical solution theory. The lack of analytical or numerical techniques with guaranteed convergence for the equilibrium problem has plagued the field and limited equilibrium analysis to rather simple auction models such as single-object auctions. Recent advances in equilibrium learning led to algorithms that find equilibrium under a wide variety of model assumptions. We analyze first- and second-price auctions where simple learning algorithms converge to an equilibrium.
The equilibrium problem in auctions is equivalent to solving an infinite-dimensional variational inequality (VI). Monotonicity and the Minty condition are the central sufficient conditions for learning algorithms to converge to an equilibrium in such VIs. We show that neither monotonicity nor pseudo- or quasi-monotonicity holds for the respective VIs. The second-price auction’s equilibrium is a Minty-type solution, but the first-price auction is not. However, the Bayes–Nash equilibrium is the unique solution to the VI within the class of uniformly increasing bid functions, which ensures that gradient-based algorithms attain the equilibrium in case of convergence, as also observed in numerical experiments.
Keywords Bayes–Nash equilibrium · variational inequality · gradient-flow algorithms 1 Introduction The Nash equilibrium is the central solution concept in non-cooperative game theory (Nash et al. 1950). Nash’s original idea was extended to games with incomplete information (Harsanyi 1967). Today, the analysis of Bayes–Nash equilibrium (BNE) is key to the study of auctions, contests, and many other economic models, where the strategic complexity for participants arises from their uncertainty about the preferences of competitors (Vickrey 1961).
Auction theory studies allocation and prices on markets with self-interested participants in equilibrium. Such predictions are important because most market institutions in this field do not have simple dominant strategies for bidding truthfully.
The celebrated Vickrey-Clarke-Groves (VCG) mechanism was shown to be unique in this respect in the widely used standard model with independent private values and quasi-linear (i.e., payoff maximizing) bidders (Green and Laffont arXiv:2311.15398v2 [cs.GT] 17 Dec 2024 1977). However, for various reasons, the VCG mechanism is rarely used in practice (Ausubel et al. 2006). Therefore, it is essential to understand non-truthful equilibrium strategies in markets more generally.
Participants in auction games do not have complete but only distributional information about the valuations of competing market participants. The value of competing bidders is modeled as a draw from an atomless distribution function. An equilibrium bid function then determines how much they bid based on their value draw and their knowledge of the prior distribution. The first-price sealed-bid auction in the symmetric and independent prior values model provides a textbook example, where the first-order conditions lead to an ordinary differential equation that admits a closed-form solution for the BNE bid function (Krishna 2009).
Unfortunately, despite the enormous academic attention auction theory has received, BNE strategies are only known for very restricted, simple market models. For bidders with non-uniform or interdependent valuation distributions, multiple objects, or non-quasilinear (i.e., non-payoff-maximizing) utility functions, we typically do not know an explicit equilibrium bid function. The equilibrium problem often leads to a system of non-linear differential equations for which we have no exact mathematical solution theory. Beyond analytical solutions, numerical techniques for solving differential equations have turned out to be challenging and have received only limited attention. Fibich and Gavish (2011) criticize the inherent numerical instability of standard techniques used in this field.
1.1 Equilibrium learning Equilibrium learning is an alternative numerical approach to finding equilibrium, as compared to standard techniques for solving differential equations. This literature examines what kind of equilibrium arises as a consequence of a relatively simple process of learning and adaptation, in which agents are trying to maximize their payoff while learning about the actions of other agents (Fudenberg and Levine 1998, Hart and Mas-Colell 2003, Young 2004). Learning provides an intuitive, tractable model of how equilibrium emerges but it is well established that independent learning dynamics do not generally obtain a Nash equilibrium (Benaim and Hirsch 1999). Numerical analyses of matrix games show that gradient-based algorithms can circle, diverge, or they are even chaotic (Sanders et al. 2018, Bielawski et al. 2021, Chotibut et al. 2020, Palaiopanos et al. 2017, Vlatakis-Gkaragkounis et al. 2023). Recently, Milionis et al. (2023) proved that there exist games, for which all game dynamics fail to converge to a Nash equilibrium from all starting points. On the other hand, there are also game classes such as potential games or games with strictly dominated strategies, where learning algorithms do converge.
1.2 Learning in auctions In recent years, a number of learning algorithms were introduced for Bayesian auction games with a continuous type and action space, and they showed convergence on a wide variety of auction models ranging from simple single-object auctions in the independent private values model to interdependent valuations and models with multiple objects (Bichler et al. 2021, 2023b). Equilibrium can be verified ex-post, but the reasons for the convergence of such learning algorithms in auction games have been a mystery so far. If auctions are indeed learnable, this has significant consequences for theory and applications alike. First, numerical solvers could be provided for models that could not be solved analytically so far. Second, if already stylized repeated auctions were not learnable, what would this mean for the growing economy of autobidding agents in display ad auctions and related applications?
What is so different in auction games compared to general-sum games, such that we see convergence in such a wide variety of models? Recently, it has been shown that a large class of learning algorithms converges in auction games with complete information, where the valuations of bidders are known a priori (Kolumbus and Nisan 2022). However, the challenge in auctions is that we have incomplete information and Bayesian models are quite different. We focus on the reasons for the convergence of learning algorithms in incomplete-information auction games.
For this, we draw on the field of operator theory and variational inequalities. Every Nash Equilibrium (NE) can be seen as a solution to a Stampacchia-type variational inequality (VI), and in some cases, the reverse is also true, for example with quasi-concave utility functions. This connection also holds for auction games and infinite-dimensional VIs (Cavazzuti et al. 2002). Interestingly, the link between Nash equilibria and VIs has been explored for traffic games (Patriksson and Rockafellar 2003) or Walrasian equilibrium (Jofré et al. 2007), but not for Bayesian games with continuous type and action space as is the case in auction theory. In contrast to finite games, auctions need to be modeled as infinite-dimensional variational inequalities.
In the literature on variational inequalities, two sufficient conditions are known, for which some types of algorithms always converge to an equilibrium. They can be seen as a generalization of convexity in optimization. The monotonicity 2 condition is the most well-known condition to guarantee convergence for VIs (Bauschke and Combettes 2017). Various first-order projection methods, as discussed by Tseng (1995), converge to a unique solution of a monotone VI, and higher-order methods have also been developed (Adil et al. 2022, Lin and Jordan 2022). Monotonicity is also central for convergence guarantees in the recent literature on learning in games (Ratliff et al. 2013, Chasnov et al. 2019).
Apart from this, the Minty condition has drawn some attention, as extragradient algorithms are known to converge to equilibrium if this condition holds globally (Strodiot et al. 2016, Song et al. 2020). This condition is also referred to as the Minty VI or dual VI of the Stampaccia-type VI (Ye 2022). In constant-sum games it is related to the celebrated smoothness condition of games (Anagnostides and Sandholm 2023) introduced by (Roughgarden 2015). It is natural to ask if the monotonicity and the Minty condition, two sufficient conditions, hold in auction games.
1.3 Contributions Demonstrating the monotonicity of auction games is challenging. Whereas practical equilibrium learning algorithms employ some form of discretization, previous research has shown that in discretized versions of auction games, the monotonicity condition is sometimes violated (Bichler et al. 2023a). However, such non-monotonicities could arise due to the game’s discretization. Violations in a discretized game might vanish in games with continuous types and actions.
That is why we study whether monotonicity or the Minty condition is satisfied in infinite dimensions in a function space.
If any of the two conditions were satisfied in function space, this would explain the convergence of algorithms also in discretized versions of the game, where the condition is violated (Glowinski et al. 1981).
First, we recover the well-known symmetric equilibrium strategies for the first-price and the second-price sealed-bid auction in the symmetric independent private-values model (Krishna 2009), but with a new proof technique based on the Gateaux derivative of the ex-ante utility function, which is novel and useful in its own right. Second, this proof technique for equilibrium problems in auctions and the resulting operator for the Gateaux derivative allows us to analyze the monotonicity and the Minty conditions.
Our findings reveal that the first- and the second-price auctions are neither monotone nor pseudo- or quasi-monotone.
Thus, we look at the Minty condition for variational inequalities. While the dominant-strategy incentive-compatible second-price auction satisfies this condition, this is not the case for the first-price auction. However, an ex-post guarantee is provided by showing the uniqueness of the VI solution (the BNE) within the class of uniformly increasing bid functions, which ensures that every gradient-based learning algorithm must converge to this solution if it does converge (within this function class). Our numerical analyses in the space of piecewise-linear functions illustrate the reasons for the Minty violations and show that they are without loss and that the gradient flows lead to the BNE in the first-price auction independent of the starting point and independent of Minty violations.
2 Related Literature More than 60 years ago, Vickrey (1961) derived the Bayes–Nash equilibrium (BNE) strategy in a single-object first-price auction in the independent-private values model with symmetric bidders, uniform prior distributions, and quasilinear utility functions. The first-order conditions, together with the assumption of symmetric bidding behavior, lead to a linear ordinary differential equation, which has a closed-form solution for the BNE bidding strategy. Unfortunately, this is only the case for the symmetric and independent private values model. It turns out that deviations from this benchmark model lead to challenges in the equilibrium analysis. For example, even in the asymmetric independent private values model, where different bidders’ values are drawn from different distributions, we get a system of non-linear differential equations; and no closed-form expression for the bidding strategies exist for general distributions (Hubbard and Paarsch 2014).
The first question is whether BNE always exists in such auction games. For finite, complete-information games, we know of the existence of a mixed Nash equilibrium (Nash et al. 1950). Glicksberg (1952) extended the existence result to games with continuous and compact action sets. For Bayesian games with continuous action space, Jackson and Swinkels (2005) provide assumptions for the existence of equilibrium in distributional strategies. For example, first-price and second-price single-unit auctions, all-pay auctions, double auctions, and multi-unit discriminatory or uniform price auctions were shown to have an equilibrium in distributional strategies, not necessarily in pure strategies.
It is interesting to note that there are auction models where there is no BNE of the continuous game, but there are equilibria in the discretized game (Jackson et al. 2002). While there was significant progress, we do not have a complete theory when a BNE exists in general continuous-type and -action auction games (Carbonell-Nicolau and McLean 2018).
Note that if one could prove the strict monotonicity of the game, this also proves the uniqueness of the equilibrium 3 in the respective auction. Therefore, we can already deduce that strict monotonicity cannot hold for the second-price auction considering asymmetric strategies, where several equilibria are known to exist (Krishna 2009, p. 118). However, we know that it is unique in the symmetric case.
Another question concerns the computational complexity in those cases where Nash equilibria do exist. Computing a Nash equilibrium in a finite, complete-information game is generally PPAD-hard (Daskalakis et al. 2009). Cai and Papadimitriou (2014) showed that finding an exact BNE in specific simultaneous auctions for multiple items is at least hard for PP, with PP being a complexity class higher than the polynomial hierarchy and close to PSPACE. Such problems can be considered intractable even for very small problem sizes. We know little about the complexity of finding BNE in other multi-item auctions. Recently, (Chen and Peng 2023) proved that there is a PTAS for approximating first-price auctions with a uniform tie-breaking rule, but that the approximation problem is PPAD-complete for other tie-breaking rules.
A related stream in the literature focuses on learning in games (Fudenberg and Levine 1998). For example, fictitious play is a natural method by which agents iteratively search for a pure Nash equilibrium and play the best response to the empirical frequency of play of other players (Brown 1951). Several algorithms have been proposed based on best or better response dynamics for finite and simultaneous-move games, and the literature is large (Abreu and Rubinstein 1988, Hart and Mas-Colell 2000, Fudenberg and Levine 1998, Hart and Mas-Colell 2003, Young 2004).
Learning dynamics do not always converge to equilibrium (Daskalakis et al. 2010, Vlatakis-Gkaragkounis et al. 2020).
Learning algorithms can cycle, diverge, or be chaotic; even in zero-sum games, where the Nash equilibrium is tractable (Mertikopoulos et al. 2018, Bailey and Piliouras 2018, Cheung and Piliouras 2020). Sanders et al. (2018) argues that chaos is typical behavior for more general large matrix games. Recent results have shown that learning dynamics do not converge in games with mixed Nash equilibria (Bailey and Piliouras 2018, Letcher et al. 2019), and that there are finite games for which any dynamics is bound to have starting points that do not end up at a Nash equilibrium (Milionis et al.
2023). Overall, the dynamics of matrix games can be arbitrarily complex and hard to characterize (Andrade et al. 2021).
It is well-known that no-external-regret learners converge to a (Bayesian) coarse correlated equilibrium, but the convergence of learning algorithms to a Nash equilibrium is only known for specific types of games such as finite potential games (Foster and Vohra 1997, Hart and Mas-Colell 2000, Jafari et al. 2001, Stoltz and Lugosi 2007, Hartline et al. 2015, Foster et al. 2016). In general, the convergence of no-regret learning algorithms to a Nash equilibrium depends on the specific structure of the game and the algorithm used. The convergence of learning algorithms to a Nash equilibrium in Bayesian auction games with continuous type and action space is largely unexplored.
We draw on the literature on variational inequalities (VI), in particular infinite-dimensional VIs. Variational inequalities were initially introduced to study equilibrium problems in physical systems (Fichera 1964, Kikuchi and Oden 1988).
Since then, the theory’s applicability has been expanded to include various problems (Lions and Stampacchia 1967, Glowinski et al. 1981, Kinderlehrer and Stampacchia 2000). Notably, the search for equilibrium in a game can be reformulated as solving a related VI. Auction models with continuous type and action space can be described as infinite-dimensional variational inequalities (Cavazzuti et al. 2002).
Monotonicity can be seen as a generalization of convexity in optimization, and it is the primary property to show the convergence of algorithms in VIs. For first-order methods Nemirovski (2004) proved that the extragradient method converges to a weak solution with a global rate of O(1/t) if the operator F is monotone and Lipschitz-continuous.
Other methods achieve the same goal (Nesterov 2007, Kotsalis et al. 2022) and achieve the lower bound of Ouyang and Xu (2021). These are also known as ”projection-type” methods. More recently, also higher-order methods were developed (Lin and Jordan 2022). There is also more recent work on non-monotone VIs, which usually assumes the existence of Minty-type solutions to the VI (Song et al. 2020, Huang and Zhang 2023). Huang and Zhang (2023) show that the existence of Minty solutions turns out to be critical in establishing convergence for the projection-type methods for non-monotone VIs.
3 Preliminaries This section lays the foundation for studying the equilibrium problem and its associated variational inequality (VI) in a function space. To begin our analysis, it is crucial to establish a derivative in function space. This requires us to work with a set of strategies that exhibit sufficient well-behaved properties. Furthermore, we narrow our focus to the symmetric setting with symmetric priors and strategies and the independent private values model. This choice simplifies our analysis and is sufficient to give answers to whether forms of monotonicity are the reason for the convergence of first-order methods in auction models.
4 3.1 Abstract setting Let n ∈N be the number of bidders. For bidder i, the set of possible bids is called Bi ⊂R, and the set of valuations of bidder i is Xi ⊂R. We define B :=× n i=1 Bi and X :=× n i=1 Xi. The goal of each bidder is to maximize their payoff, i.e., they consider their utility function ui : B × X →R : ui(b, x).
For this, they search for a strategy βi : X →Bi. Let the vector space Vi contain all possible strategies βi, while the subset Bi ⊂Vi contains all admissible strategies, and we define V :=× n i=1 Vi and B :=× n i=1 Bi. The random values Xi of all bidders i = 1, . . . , n are distributed in Xi according to an atomless probability distribution Fi with full support over Xi. We denote by Ui : V →R : Ui(β) := EX[ui(β(X), X)] the expected utility of bidder i for given strategies β. Note that here and in the following, we denote by β a vector (β1, β2, . . . , βn) and by βi, β∗ −i the vector (β∗ 1, . . . , β∗ i−1, βi, β∗ i+1, . . . , β∗ n). The Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE) for this auction game is then given by: Problem 1 (BNE). Find β∗= (β∗ 1, . . . , β∗ n) ∈B such that for all i = 1, . . . , n there holds Ui(β∗) ≥Ui(βi, β∗ −i) ∀βi ∈Bi.
(1) Under certain conditions (to be elaborated in the following), the equilibrium condition can be reformulated as a variational inequality. For this, we need to consider the expected utility function’s derivative in a function space. This demands some regularity of the underlying function space. Assume Vi is a Banach space and denote by V ∗ i := L(Vi, R) its dual space consisting of all continuous linear functionals on Vi. Note that not all linear functionals are continuous for general infinite-dimensional spaces. Furthermore, assume that Bi ⊂Vi is convex and closed. Following the standard procedure in the literature (Lions and Stampacchia 1967, Kinderlehrer and Stampacchia 2000), we derive the so-called Gateaux-derivative of Ui, which can be understood as the generalization of the (linear) directional derivative in normed spaces. So, let DUi(β)[d] denote the directional derivative of Ui at β = (β1, . . . , βn) ∈B with respect to βi along d ∈Vi, i.e., DUi(β)[d] := lim ε→0 ε−1�Ui(βi + εd, β−i) −Ui(β)  ∀d ∈Vi.
(2) The directional derivative is the Gateaux-derivative iff DUi(β) ∈V ∗ i , i. e., when the derivative is a continuous linear operator in the direction d ∈Vi. If the Gateaux-derivative exists, a necessary condition for a BNE is the following (Stampacchia-type) VI (Kinderlehrer and Stampacchia 2000): Problem 2 (VI). Find β∗∈B such that for all i = 1, . . . , n there holds DUi(β∗)[βi −β∗ i ] ≤0 ∀βi ∈Bi.
(3) A sufficient condition, also referred to as the dual VI of the Stampacchia formulation, is given by the (Minty-type) VI: Problem 3 (MVI). Find β∗∈B which satisfies for all i = 1, . . . , n Di(β)[βi −β∗ i ] ≤0 ∀β ∈B.
(4) In general, solutions of the Minty-type VI (4) are a subset of the BNEs given by (1), which are, in turn, a subset of solutions of the Stampacchia-type VI (3). Vice versa, solutions of the Stampacchia-type VI (3) are also BNEs if Ui is pseudoconvex in βi for all β−i, and BNEs are, in turn, solutions of the Minty-type VI (4) if Ui is quasiconvex in βi for all β−i (Cavazzuti et al. 2002).
3.2 Symmetric and independent private value auctions In the following sections, we consider second- and first-price sealed-bid auctions under the assumption of (complete) symmetry and identically independently distributed private values. (Complete) symmetry implies Bi = B, Xi = X, Xi ∼iid. Fi ≡F, ui ≡u ∀i = 1, . . . , n.
Furthermore, private values ensure βi(x) = βi(xi) for i = 1, . . . , n, i.e., the strategy of each bidder i depends only on the knowledge of their own valuation Xi = xi. The ex-ante utility is denoted U(β) := EX[u(β(X), X)], and symmetric strategies are denoted ˜ β := (˜ β, . . . , ˜ β) ∈B for ˜ β ∈B.
In the following, we assume X = [0, 1] (without loss of generality) and F ∈C0,1([0, 1]), i.e., the cumulative probability function is Lipschitz-continuous. To analyze the VI we have to define an appropriate set of admissible strategies. This 5 set should be sufficiently general to allow for strategies that may be considered as sensible for the underlying problem.
Additionally, it needs to provide adequate structure, e.g., an inner product or a natural dual product. Therefore, consider the Banach space Vi = V := W 1,1(0, 1; F) = {β ∈L1(0, 1; F) | β′ ∈L1(0, 1; F)}, i.e., V consists of F-integrable functions with F-integrable weak derivatives. The figure shows that violations of the Minty condition, a sufficient condition for convergence, are without loss in this analysis. The laminar flows take a turn, but no matter with which parameter combination one starts, the gradient flow always leads to the Bayes–Nash equilibrium. Traversing the red area means that the strategies analyzed on the way move away from the Bayes–Nash equilibrium, but they move closer again once the algorithm steps outside this area.1 7 Conclusions Learning in games has received much recent attention in the literature. It is well known, that learning algorithms do not always converge to an equilibrium in games, but they do converge in some types such as potential games.
Recent advances in equilibrium learning showed that learning algorithms converge in a wide variety of auction games.
The reasons for these observations are not well understood. We draw on the connection between auction games and infinite-dimensional variational inequalities, which has not been explored so far. In particular, there are sufficient conditions for which it has been shown that independent optimization algorithms find a solution to the variational inequality.
Monotonicity can be seen as a generalization of convexity in optimization, and it provides a condition for first-order optimization methods to converge to a solution of the variational inequality. Our analysis shows that neither the second- nor the first-price auctions are monotonous. There are even counterexamples for the weaker pseudo- and quasi-monotonicity conditions. More recent literature on non-monotone variational inequality uses the Minty condition to show the convergence of extragradient algorithms (cf. Appendix A). In the first-price auction, this condition is also not satisfied, even when assuming a uniform prior.
However, both auctions have a unique solution to the variational inequality (in case of first-price auctions up to the boundary), which means, that every gradient-based learning algorithm must attain the Bayes–Nash equilibrium (BNE) if it does converge. Regarding this problem as a dynamical system provides a potential remedy. Since the BNE is the only stationary point (in the interior), the gradient dynamics either converge to the BNE, converge to a limit cycle, or diverge.
In general, finding limit cycles of dynamical systems is a PSPACE-complete problem (Papadimitriou and Vishnoi 2015).
Our numerical explorations illustrate that the gradient dynamics do converge in the first- and second-price auctions.
Whether limit cycles or divergence are possible in other auction games, remains an open research question to be studied in the future.

This academic paper by Bichler et al. (Technical University of Munich, December 18, 2024) investigates why learning algorithms converge to equilibrium in Bayesian auction games, analyzing this through the lens of variational inequalities (VIs) and operator theory. The authors focus on symmetric first- and second-price sealed-bid auctions under the independent private values model.

Key findings:
- The equilibrium problem in auctions is equivalent to solving an infinite-dimensional VI.
- Neither monotonicity nor pseudo- or quasi-monotonicity holds for the Gateaux derivative operators in either first- or second-price auctions (even with simple two-bidder uniform prior cases).
- The second-price auction's equilibrium satisfies the Minty-type condition (MVI), but the first-price auction does not—violations occur even locally around the BNE.
- Despite these violations, the Bayes-Nash equilibrium (BNE) is the unique solution to the VI within the class of uniformly increasing bid functions, ensuring that any gradient-based learning algorithm that converges must converge to the BNE.
- Numerical analysis with piecewise-linear bid functions shows that Minty violations are "without loss"—gradient flows still lead to the BNE regardless of starting point.
- The authors provide novel proofs of existence and uniqueness using Gateaux derivatives, and derive explicit expressions for the directional derivatives of the utility functions.

The paper concludes that the convergence of learning algorithms in auction games is not explained by standard sufficient conditions (monotonicity, Minty condition) but rather by the uniqueness of the VI solution, which makes the BNE the only stationary point in the interior of the strategy space. Whether limit cycles or divergence are possible in other auction games remains an open question.

# Asymmetry and revenue in first-price auctions

Author links open overlay panel Harrison Cheng

Show more

Add to Mendeley

## Abstract

We show by an example that in first-price IPV auctions, asymmetry in bidders' valuations need not reduce the revenue compared to a benchmark symmetric model with the same amount of social surplus. Asymmetry need not reduce competition in first-price auctions.

### Research Highlights

► In first-price auctions, asymmetry in bidder valuations need not reduce revenue. ► An example with discrete values or continuous values is shown. ►Asymmetry in valuations need not weaken competition in first-price auctions.

## Introduction

Bidders are asymmetric when their values have different probability distributions. Most of the literatures in auctions focus on symmetric auctions. However asymmetric auctions are quite wide spread and many issues involve asymmetric auctions. For example, even if bidders are initially symmetric, the possibility of joint bidding and merger among bidders makes it necessary to study asymmetric auctions as in Waehrer (1999), Waehrer and Perry (2003), Marshall et al. (1994), Dalkir et al. (2000). Information revelation can also make the auctions asymmetric, as in Landsberger et al. (2001) and Haile (2001). Asymmetric auctions also arise naturally in issues related to procurements as in Tan (1992) and Arozamena and Cantillon (2004).

In private value auctions, Cantillon (2008) studied how asymmetry may affect revenue compared to a benchmark symmetric model with the same social surplus. The idea is that in the IPV auctions, competition may be more intensive when bidder values are more similar, leading to higher revenue for the auctioneer. This intuition is confirmed in her paper in a general model with second-price auctions. Cantillon (2008) also studied a similar question in first-price auctions which are often used in procurement auctions. She obtained the same result for three classes of value distributions in first-price auctions. Furthermore, for the class of power function distributions for which the degree of asymmetry can be properly defined, the seller's revenue is lower when there is more asymmetry and the total surplus is kept constant. In numerical experiments using truncated normal distributions, the result is quite robust to numerical specifications, leading her to suggest that it may hold for more general distributions. This remains an open question.

We will show by an example that in first-price IPV auctions, the asymmetry effect on revenue is less general when the benchmark is defined as in Cantillon (2008). The example has discrete values, but it can be approximated by a continuum model with the same conclusion using the upper hemicontinuity of the equilibrium correspondence established by Lebrun (2002). Our use of discrete models to illustrate the comparisons of revenues is very similar to that of Maskin and Riley (1985). Different kinds of benchmark comparisons were made in Kaplan, and Zamir (2002) based on information structures, in which it is also possible to have higher revenue in asymmetric first-price auctions.

Cantillon's result held for several distribution classes and appeared robust across numerical experiments. However, Cheng demonstrates through a counterexample that this conclusion is not universal for first-price auctions.

The example involves two bidders with discrete value distributions: Bidder 1 has values 0 or 1 (with probability 0.45 for 0), and Bidder 2 has values 0 or 12/11 (with probability 0.4 for 0). Advantage for Sale: Endogenous Asymmetry in Sequential Auctions ∗ Maur´ ıcio Bugarin Universidade de Bras´ ılia Odilon Cˆ amara† University of Southern California Wilfredo L. Maldonado Universidade de S˜ ao Paulo October 5, 2025 Abstract In some real-world markets where buyers compete to trade with a seller, the winner of the good or service today also gains a contractual advantage in future competitions.
We study advantage-for-sale (AFS) mechanisms, where the seller deliberately grants this advantage.
We characterize the optimal AFS mechanism and show it strictly benefits the seller when she has limited ability to contract on past outcomes. The seller grants a larger advantage when bidders are fewer or more patient. This advantage—a lower reserve price and a discount on rival bids—intensifies competition for the winner’s status and increases revenue.
∗A previous draft of this paper circulated with the title “Endogenous Asymmetry in Sequential Auctions.” The authors are grateful to Gonzalo Cisternas, Ren´ e Kirkegaard, Vijay Krishna, Jo˜ ao Ramos, Gil Riella, Kathryn Spier, and the participants of the 2025 World Congress (Econometric Society), 10th Latin American Workshop in Law and Economics, and the 2024 European Winter Meeting of the Econometric Society for their valuable discussions and suggestions. The authors contributed equally and are listed in alphabetical order.
All opinions and any remaining errors are the sole responsibility of the authors. Maldonado acknowledges the financial support of the CNPq 302856/2022-6 and 402949/2021-8, Funda¸ c˜ ao de Amparo ` a Pesquisa do Estado de S˜ ao Paulo (FAPESP) 2023/07274-0, and Funda¸ c˜ ao Instituto de Pesquisas Econˆ omicas (FIPE) †Corresponding author: ocamara@marshall.usc.edu 1 Introduction Many market mechanisms in which potential buyers compete to trade with a seller, or suppli-ers compete for a buyer, have a recurring nature. For example, a significant portion of public procurement is conducted through periodic auctions. Moreover, many market mechanisms feature contracts that give the previous winner some formal advantage in the next competi-tion. Such rights are common in various contexts, including real estate transactions (where tenants may hold a statutory right of first refusal to match a third-party offer), corporate agreements (where minority shareholders may have preemptive rights to purchase additional shares before outsiders), and intellectual property contracts (where licensees may negotiate clauses granting them renewal or expansion rights before the asset is offered to others). Some of these advantages are exogenously imposed on buyers and sellers (mandated by law), while others are endogenously included in the contracts.1 There are different reasons why a seller might want to give an advantage to the previous winner. For example, if a landlord incurs fixed costs when switching tenants, then she might find it optimal to give an advantage to the current tenant when the lease is up for renewal. In this paper, we study a different rationale. We show that it can be optimal to offer a contract that gives an advantage to the previous winner when the seller faces limited commitment: when auction rules cannot depend on a detailed history of past outcomes.
To clearly present our insights, we consider a simple infinitely repeated game in which one seller has one object (or service) to sell at each period. There are n symmetric buyers who at each period privately draw an i.i.d. value for the good, where the distribution F satisfies the monotone hazard rate condition. Players discount future payoffs by δ. We study a class of mechanisms called advantage-for-sale (AFS), in which allocation and transfer rules in each period may depend on the identity of the buyer who won the good in the previous period, but not on other past outcomes. The previous winner may receive a pre-specified advantage in the current auction—potentially in allocation, pricing, or both—while all other bidders (the losers) are treated symmetrically. Thus, the mechanism creates an “advantage” that is 1In a recent example, UFC committed to provide content to Paramount during the next seven years for $7.7 billion and awarded them future advantages when content rights are up for renewal (https://www.cnbc.
com/2025/08/11/paramount-buys-ufc-rights-skydance-merger.html).
1 then put “for sale.” The seller’s problem is to design the AFS mechanism that maximizes the expected per-period revenue. Our main questions are: is creating a winner’s advantage profitable? If so, then what should be the optimal advantage?2 As a benchmark, in a one-period model, (standard) virtual value functions are v −1 −F(v) f(v) .
(1) If the seller does not value the good, then it is optimal to sell it to the bidder with the highest virtual value above zero, and keep the good if all virtual values are negative. The seller cares about extracting surplus from bidders, but she does not care about how the surplus is allocated across different symmetric bidders. The seller can implement this mechanism as a second-price auction with an optimal reserve price. Consequently, whenever the good is sold it is sold to the bidder with the highest value.
In contrast, at each period t, we prove that the optimal AFS mechanism assigns to the winner of period t −1 an adjusted virtual value v −(1 −δ)1 −F(v) f(v) , (2) and to all other bidders an adjusted virtual value v −  1 + δ n −1  1 −F(v) f(v) .
(3) Hence, the seller introduces handicaps (Es˝ o and Szentes, 2007) to increase the adjusted virtual value of the previous winner and decrease that of the losers. The optimal allocation is to give the good to the bidder with the highest adjusted virtual value above zero, and keep the good if all adjusted virtual values are negative. This mechanism creates a modified second-price auction in which the previous winner has a lower reserve price and can obtain the good at a discounted price.
Our results provide a series of relevant insights. First, we emphasize the tradeoff faced by the seller.
In this optimal allocation, the previous winner is more likely to purchase today’s good and he pays a lower price. Sometimes he purchases even though he does not have the highest value v. Therefore, the seller distorts the benchmark one-period allocation and loses some potential revenue from this misallocation. However, forward-looking bidders 2The same questions arise when a buyer designs procurement auctions.
2 understand the value of winning the advantage; hence, they all increase their bids. A priori, it is not clear which effect dominates. Moreover, bidders pay today for a future benefit, and the value of this benefit is endogenous to bidding choices. We show that the net effect is positive — the optimal AFS mechanism increases expected revenues. One way to view this result is that our seller has one additional degree of freedom to extract surplus from bidders: she can transfer future surplus from the losers to the winner, which incentivizes bidders to bid more aggressively.
A second insight comes from the discount factor. The adjusted virtual value (2) of the advantaged bidder increases in δ: it is “cheaper” for the seller to satisfy the advantaged bidder’s IC constraint when players are more patient. The intuition is the following. Future information rents received by the advantaged bidder are partially compensated today by an increase in how much bidders are willing to pay to win the auction. If tomorrow the seller will give a $1 additional benefit to today’s winner, then this cost is partially offset by the corresponding δ$1 increase in revenues from current bids. It is fully offset when δ →1, in which case (2) becomes the true value v without any discount (the winner’s IC constraint can be satisfied “for free”). Moreover, because v is not negative, the seller never keeps the good in this limiting case. The converse is true for losers: their adjusted virtual values are decreasing in δ. If disadvantaged players receive more information rents tomorrow, then this loss is compounded by a lower revenue today because the winning advantage becomes smaller. Consequently, as players become more patient, the seller optimally implements a mechanism that gives to the winner a bigger advantage: he is more likely to win again, will pay lower future prices, and winning spells become longer.
The third insight relates to the benefit of rewarding winners and penalizing losers. For any δ ∈(0, 1), the adjusted virtual value (2) of the previous winner is not a function of n, while the losers’ adjusted virtual values (3) are strictly increasing in n. When n is small, previous losers are penalized twice — their adjusted virtual values are more likely to be negative (higher reservation price), and they become smaller relative to the adjusted virtual value of the previous winner.
When n is small, the seller benefits from intensifying the asymmetry because it increases the endogenous net value of winning each auction by more than the loss from the misallocation (giving the good to the advantaged player when there is another bidder with a higher value).
3 A fourth insight is that the optimal AFS mechanism is related to an auxiliary mechanism design problem. In the limiting case δ →1 and n →∞, the optimal allocation in our problem looks as if the winner of the period t −1 auction gains the period t −1 good (without the possibility of resale), and at the same time gains the period t good with the option of reselling it using an optimal auction. The advantaged player keeps the good if the (standard) virtual value of all other bidders are below his own realized value v, otherwise the good goes to the disadvantaged bidder with the highest value. By “selling” the period t good to the winner of the period t −1 auction, the seller reduces the loss from the information rent (when bidding in period t −1, the winner does not know his period-t value) and she later uses the realized period-t value of the advantaged bidder to implement an optimal resale auction. We can compare this to classic principal-agent problems in which the best contract for the principal is to “sell the firm” to the agent, by charging a fixed fee upfront and letting the agent become the residual claimant.
Fifth, we can connect our results to multi-period contracts of an indivisible service, such as the owner of an intellectual or physical property choosing licensing/leasing terms, or a professional athlete signing with a team.
We define conditions such that the optimal AFS mechanism resembles a leasing contract featuring three components: a fixed per-period payment, a signing bonus, and explicit conditions for triggering a renegotiation.
These conditions define that the seller only renegotiates the lease terms if a competing bidder offers a sufficiently high signing bonus. At this point, the current lessee can keep the lease if he pays a re-signing bonus that is a discounted price on the competing offer.
Our paper contributes to the literature on contracting when agents’ private information changes over time, which started with Baron and Besanko (1984) — see Bergemann and Said (2010) and Bergemann and V¨ alim¨ aki (2019) for a review of dynamic mechanism design.
Riordan and Sappington (1987) consider a regulator who auctions a monopoly franchise with the goal of maximizing consumers’ welfare. The regulator allows the winning producer to charge prices above marginal cost; this ex post distortion results in more competitive bids ex ante. Similarly, our seller distorts future allocations in order to foster more competitive bids.
Related work on revenue-maximizing dynamic sales include Courty and Li (2000), Battaglini (2005), and Boleslavsky and Said (2013).
In Es˝ o and Szentes (2007), buyers have private information and the seller can release 4 additional signals that affect buyers’ valuations. The optimal mechanism can be implemented by a handicap auction: in the first round, buyers purchase price premiums that influence the second round prices and allocation rules. They show the importance of orthogonalization (distinguishing between initial and subsequent private information). Board (2007) and other papers also find optimal mechanisms that feature virtual values adjusted by a handicap. In a very general mechanism design setting, Pavan et al. (2014) derive the handicap from impulse response functions that capture how agents’ types evolve over discrete time. This becomes the stochastic flow process in the continuous time model of Bergemann and Strack (2015).
In these papers, at the beginning of the game, the designer commits to allocation rules that can depend on the entire history of all past announcements. Moreover, buyers’ partici-pation constraints only need to be satisfied in the initial period (buyers commit to participate in all future periods). To extract surplus, the seller combines an entry fee with the optimal handicap, which may be fixed or time-varying, depending on the model. A buyer who chooses not to join the mechanism in the first period can be punished with a zero continuation payoff (he can be effectively banned from all future auctions). We complement this literature by considering a constrained seller: the only past information that she can use is the identity of the previous winner. Hence, buyers who do not participate in the auction today cannot be banned from future auctions and their participation constraint must be satisfied in every period.3 We show how our constrained seller can use this state variable (the identity of the previous winner) to design a handicap that leads all buyers to bid more aggressively, even though this state variable is not correlated with future valuations.
We also contribute to the literature on dynamic mechanism design in environments where the designer has limited commitment. Recent examples include Bester and Strausz (2001), Battaglini (2007), Skreta (2006, 2015), Deb and Said (2015), Liu et al. (2019), Gerardi and Maestri (2020), and Doval and Skreta (2022, 2024). Most papers focus on a designer who is unable to commit to long-term contracts. Our focus is on a designer who can only 3Kr¨ ahmer and Strausz (2015) study sequential screening when the seller must satisfy buyers’ ex post (instead of ex ante) participation constraints. In the two-period model of Baron and Besanko (1984), if the agent’s type is independent across periods, the principal can implement the efficient allocation in the second-period and extract the resulting surplus via a first-period fee. The key assumption is that the principal commits to not trade with the agent in the second period if he did not accept the contract in the first period.
5 condition auction rules on a limited set of past outcome variables. In this paper, we study the case in which the only past information that can be used by the designer is the identity of the previous winner. Arguably, the identity of the previous winner is an easier variable to contract on than other details from past auctions; hence, this is an important scenario to study partial commitment. But most importantly, this is an empirically relevant state variable as many contracts grant special treatment to incumbents in future renegotiation processes.
Our paper also contributes to the literature on sequential auctions (Chakraborty, 2018, 2019; Salant and Cabral, 2019), which studies dynamic formats under standard rules but does not consider asymmetry creation as a design variable.
Moreover, the literature on auction asymmetries has largely focused on environments where asymmetries are exogenous, either through differing value distributions (Maskin and Riley, 2000; Cantillon, 2008) or through asymmetries in information (Xu and Cavallo, 2022). Recent contributions explore how asymmetries may arise endogenously from bidders’ actions (Cisternas and Figueroa, 2015; De Silva et al., 2005). However, in these settings, asymmetries emerge indirectly from bidders’ behavior rather than from the seller’s strategic design.
Another related literature studies how sellers can grant preferential treatment to specific bidders through contractual devices such as first-dealer-first-refusal (FDFR) or right-of-first-refusal (ROFR) provisions. Bikhchandani et al. (2005) highlight that ROFR may reduce seller revenue and may lead to inefficiencies. Burguet and Perry (2009) show how a bilateral negotiation between the buyer and one of the suppliers can increase their joint surplus and characterize the optimal one-period auction. Unlike our optimal allocation, their allocation is not a function of the discount factor (because there is a single auction) and the number of buyers (because they consider a bilateral negotiation rather than an auction). Burguet and Perry (2014) consider a one-period procurement with two bidders who compete for an exogenously determined ROFR advantage. In turn, we characterize the optimal endogenous advantage, with n bidders and repeated auctions.
The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the model. Our main results are in Section 3. Section 4 describes a simpler alternative mechanism, the price-matching second-price auction, and shows when it is better than standard auctions. Section 5 concludes. Omitted proofs are in the Appendix.
6 2 The Model 2.1 Overview We consider a repeated game with infinite periods and n + 1 risk-neutral players: one seller and n ≥2 potential buyers (bidders). All players discount future payoffs by δ ∈[0, 1). At each period, the seller has one unit of an indivisible, non-durable good for sale. The seller has no value for the good4 and wants to maximize her per-period expected revenue. At the beginning of the game, the seller selects one auction mechanism M, from a set M of auction mechanisms, which we define shortly. The mechanism M defines the auction rules, which must be the same across periods.
At the beginning of each period, each buyer i ∈N = {1, . . . , n} privately draws a new value vi for the good. Values are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) across buyers and across periods, according to the cumulative distribution function F(v), with continuous probability density function f(v), which has full support on the set V ≡[v, v], 0 ≤v < v < ∞; f(v) > 0, ∀v ∈V . To streamline presentation, assume that F satisfies the monotone hazard rate (MHR) condition, f(v)/(1−F(v)) is non-decreasing. Let v = (v1, . . . , vn) ∈V ≡ V n be a realized vector of values, which has distribution F (v) = Qn i=1 F(vi) and density f(v).
Define v−i ∈V −i ≡V n−1 as the vector excluding bidder i, with corresponding distributions F −i(v−i) and f −i(v−i).
Buyers cannot resell the good. The period-t utility of buyer i equals vi if he acquires the good on period t, zero if he does not acquire the good, minus any monetary transfers to the seller in that period. Each buyer wants to maximize his discounted expected utility.
2.2 Advantage-for-Sale Mechanism We study a tractable and empirically relevant class of dynamic auction mechanisms. We define an Advantage-for-Sale (AFS) mechanism as a dynamic mechanism in which the auction allocation and transfer rules in each period t may depend on the identity of the buyer who won the auction in period t −1. The mechanism offers a well-defined advantage for the previous winner, which shapes an endogenous asymmetry in the current auction.
4It is straightforward to extend the model and consider a seller with a constant value v0 ≥0 for the good.
7 To simplify the analysis, the seller’s choice is constrained by the following rules. First, we focus on direct revelation mechanisms where at the beginning of each period t all buyers simultaneously announce their period-t value. Second, allocation and monetary transfers related to the period-t auction cannot be delayed to later periods or depend on future actions and outcomes. Third, period-t auction rules can depend on the identity of the period-(t −1) winner but not on other details of past bids or past outcomes. Fourth, we assume that, if the good is not sold in period t, then the bidder who has the advantage in period t retains the advantage in period t + 1.

Our equilibrium concept is Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium (PBE). The seller’s strategy is to choose the mechanism M ∈M that maximizes the expected per-period revenue. Therefore, if δ = 0, then a symmetric auction is optimal: the seller allocates the good to the bidder with the highest value vi if his virtual value is positive, otherwise the seller keeps the good. When δ > 0, the second term implies that the seller may benefit from implementing an asymmetric auction that provides an advantage to the winner of the previous period. The fundamental tradeoffs are the following. In each period t, to give an advantage to the previous winner, the seller sometimes inefficiently allocates the good — gives the good to the previous winner when there is another bidder with a higher value. This misallocation increases U W and decreases U L, making all bidders willing to bid more to gain the advantage ∆U. This misallocation increases the second term in (17) but decreases the first term. Moreover, the seller could implement a lower reserve price for the previous winner and a higher reserve price for the previous losers, increasing the second term in (17) at the cost of decreasing the first term.
It is then not clear a priori if the net value of increasing the second term and decreasing the first is positive. We prove that the seller strictly benefits from the optimal asymmetric 12 mechanism.
Moreover, as players become more patient (higher δ), the seller makes the auction more asymmetric to increase the winner’s advantage.

The seller now has one important additional degree of freedom to increase her payoff: she gains from shifting payoff from the losers to the winner.

As an interesting application, interpret the seller as someone providing an indivisible service each period. Suppose the service is always valuable (v > 0), the reserve price binds in a one-period auction (vf(v) < 1), and players are patient (δ > 1−vf(v)). These conditions guarantee that the adjusted virtual value of the previous winner is always positive and that of the losers is strictly negative for v. The optimal AFS mechanism resembles a leasing contract featuring three components: a fixed rent, a signing bonus, and conditions for renegotiation.
The buyer receiving the service must pay the fixed amount v + δ∆p each period he receives the service. For buyer i, the gross value of receiving the service (and the future advantage) at this price is vi+δ∆p. Therefore, this fixed rental price yields a positive net payoff, vi−v. If a competitor wants to take the lease from the incumbent buyer, he must offer a signing bonus.
At each period, each disadvantaged bidder offers to pay a signing bonus vi −v, plus the fixed rent v + δ∆p. The auction rule establishes that only sufficiently high signing bonuses can trigger a renegotiation (vi must yield a positive adjusted virtual value). If no signing offer is above this reserve price, then the incumbent keeps the service and only pays the fixed price.
If at least one offer is above the reserve price, then the incumbent has the opportunity to make a counteroffer. Let v′ be the lowest value such that cω(v′|ω) ≥ci(vmax|ω ̸= i), where vmax is the value of the highest competitor. To keep the lease, the incumbent must offer a resigning bonus v′ −v, which is strictly lower than the competitor’s best offer vmax −v. If vω ≥v′, then the incumbent makes this minimum counteroffer, pays the fixed rent, and keeps the service. Otherwise, the seller ends the current lease and starts serving the competitor.

In this section, we present a simpler AFS mechanism that belongs to the set of mechanisms M but does not depend on these parameters and does not have a reserve price. Of course, this mechanism is not as profitable as the one from the previous section, but we show that it is better than a standard second-price auction without a reserve price (SP auction), when players are sufficiently patient. The logic behind this result reinforces insights from our main model.
Define a price-matching second-price auction (PM auction) as follows.
Let ω be the identity of the advantaged bidder, and assume that n ≥3. At each period, the seller first runs a standard second-price auction without a reserve price, but only includes in the auction the n −1 bidders who do not have the advantage. This auction results in some price y (the second highest bid) and an interim winner (the player with the highest bid). Then the seller offers to bidder ω the choice: he can purchase the good and keep the advantage in the next period if he pays y; otherwise, the good and the advantage go to the interim winner.
We start by characterizing equilibrium bidding strategies. Suppose the seller uses a PM auction. Let U PM W be the discounted expected value of a bidder who is starting the period as the winner of the previous auction, and U PM L the corresponding value for a loser. The premium for becoming a winner is ∆U PM ≡U PM W −U PM L . For each player, the present value of winning the auction is vi + δU PM W , and that of losing the auction is δU PM L . The proof first shows that the endogenous wining advantage ∆U PM depends on n and F, but not on δ. This is perhaps surprising because increasing δ increases the gross value of winning the advantage (since players today care more about future advantages). However, a higher δ increases how much players need to pay to win the advantage — all players bid more aggressively. These two effects cancel out and the endogenous winning value becomes a constant. This is consistent with our previous results: fixed the allocation rule p, the winning advantage (22) is not a function of δ.
Consequently, in the PM auction, the per-period expected revenue is a linear function of δ. If δ = 0, then the PM auction is strictly worse — consumers do not increase their bids because they do not value the future. If vf(v) > 1, then the best independent auction is the SP auction (the seller does not benefit from reserve prices). The corollary follows from Proposition 1 when δ > ˜ δ.

These clauses allow a favored bidder to match any competing offer made for the target company. In 2024, the Brazilian National Treasury launched the New Program for Expanding the Investor Base in Treasury Direct Auctions. The program’s novelty lies in its sequential design: winners of the 2025 auctions will hold a competitive advantage in the 2026 auctions.

In particular, when the seller cannot punish buyers for not participating in past auctions. These constraints can be relevant in practi-cal cases that involve governments or firms that are limited in their ability to commit to long-run contracts with multiple potential buyers. In these cases, the seller benefits from transferring future surplus from losers to the winner because it incentivizes buyers to bid more aggressively. We show how the optimal AFS mechanism introduces auction handicaps that are beneficial to the winner and detrimental to the losers.
Under some conditions, the optimal AFS mechanism resembles a leasing contract fea-turing three components: a fixed rent, a signing bonus, and conditions for renegotiation.

args.summary:
This academic paper by Bugarin, Câmara, and Maldonado (October 2025) studies "advantage-for-sale" (AFS) mechanisms in sequential auctions, where the seller deliberately grants the previous winner a contractual advantage in future competitions. The authors consider an infinitely repeated game with one seller and n symmetric buyers who draw i.i.d. private values each period. The seller can only condition auction rules on the identity of the previous winner (not on other past outcomes).

**Key Findings:**

1. **Optimal Mechanism**: The seller optimally assigns adjusted virtual values: the previous winner gets v - (1-δ)(1-F(v))/f(v), while losers get v - (1 + δ/(n-1))(1-F(v))/f(v). This creates a modified second-price auction where the winner has a lower reserve price and a discount on rival bids.

2. **Revenue Impact**: The AFS mechanism strictly increases expected revenue compared to independent auctions by transferring future surplus from losers to the winner, incentivizing all bidders to bid more aggressively.

3. **Discount Factor (δ)**: As players become more patient (δ → 1), the seller grants a larger advantage. The winner's adjusted virtual value increases in δ, making it "cheaper" to satisfy the winner's incentive compatibility constraint.

4. **Number of Bidders (n)**: When n is small, the seller intensifies the asymmetry between winner and losers, as the losers' adjusted virtual values are strictly increasing in n.

5. **Practical Implementation**: Under certain conditions, the optimal AFS mechanism resembles a leasing contract with a fixed rent, a signing bonus, and renegotiation conditions triggered by competing offers.

6. **Price-Matching Auction**: The authors also study a simpler alternative (PM auction) that does not depend on distribution parameters. This auction outperforms standard second-price auctions when players are sufficiently patient (δ > δ̃).

The paper contributes to dynamic mechanism design, sequential auctions, and the literature on contractual advantages (e.g., right of first refusal). The optimal mechanism features endogenous asymmetry that intensifies competition for the winner's status.

## Abstract

Bidders' asymmetries are widespread in auction markets. Yet, their impact on behavior and, ultimately, revenue and profits is still not well understood. In this paper, I define a natural benchmark auction environment to which to compare any private value auction with asymmetrically distributed valuations. I show that the expected revenue from the benchmark auction always dominates that from the asymmetric auction, both in the first price auction and the second price auction. These results formalize and make transparent the idea that competition is reduced by bidders' asymmetries. The paper also contributes to a better understanding of competition and the nature of rents in auction markets. Anonymity of the allocation mechanism seems to be an important factor.

args.summary:
This is a RePEc/IDEAS webpage for the academic paper "The effect of bidders' asymmetries on expected revenue in auctions" by Estelle Cantillon, published in Games and Economic Behavior (Elsevier), vol. 62(1), pages 1-25, January 2008.

**Abstract Summary:** The paper examines how bidder asymmetries (common in auction markets) impact behavior, revenue, and profits. The author defines a benchmark auction environment to compare against any private value auction with asymmetrically distributed valuations. Key findings: expected revenue from the benchmark auction always dominates that from the asymmetric auction, in both first-price and second-price auctions. The results formalize the idea that competition is reduced by bidder asymmetries. The paper also explores the nature of competition and rents in auction markets, noting that anonymity of the allocation mechanism appears to be an important factor.

**Author:** Estelle Cantillon (registered with RePEc).

**Other versions:** The paper is also available as a ULB Institutional Repository working paper (2013/9001) and a Cowles Foundation Discussion Paper (1279).

**JEL Classification:** D40 (Market Structure, Pricing, and Design - General), D44 (Auctions), L13 (Oligopoly and Other Imperfect Markets).

The page also lists 22 references, 63 citations, and 20 related items, along with metadata for corrections and download information.

Scoring and Favoritism in Optimal Procurement Design Pasha Andreyanov Ilya Krasikov Alex Suzdaltsev HSE University September 4, 2023 Scoring auctions § Scoring auctions are widely used for procurement in many countries § In a scoring auction, potential sellers submit multidimensional price-quality bids and then the buyer selects a winner using some predetermined scoring rule (a formula that converts a multidimensional bid into a single number) § Example: “A+B” auctions for road construction in California, where “A” is price and “B2 is speed of construction § A popular choice of the scoring rule is a quasilinear score Spq, pq “ spqq ´ p (q is quality, p is price) Che (1993) § In an influential paper (Che, 1993), Che proves that in a “standard” setting (one-dimensional types, symmetry, well-behaved cost and utility functions) a scoring auction with a carefully chosen quasilinear scoring rule is a buyer-optimal mechanism for procurement § The optimal quality score function s˚pqq is not equal to true buyer’s utility vpqq; s˚pqq is flatter than vpqq - The buyer wants to depress firms’ incentives to increase quality relative to the efficient level in order to save on information rents § So far much of theoretical literature on scoring auctions largely follows Che’s framework (e.g., Branco (1997), Asker and Cantillon (2008), Asker and Cantillon (2010), Nishimura (2015)) Our focus: Investment costs § Importantly, in the current literature following Che (1993), it is assumed that only the winner of the contract incurs costs cpq, θq - In other words, all costs are production costs § In contrast, in reality a substantial share of costs has to be incurred before the scoring auction, i.e. by every participant - Developing and improving the product - Gaining experience - Gathering information § I.e., real-world scoring auctions inevitably have an all-pay component – investment costs that have to be incurred regardless of winning § Also, these investments are independent, in that a firm’s investment may not depend on other firms’ private information § Q: How would an optimal mechanism for procurement change in such an environment?
Plan for today: 1. I will show a full characterization of optimal symmetric mechanisms when there are both production and investment costs including the optimal scoring formula 2. I will show a number of results saying that in general the optimal mechanism in our setting is asymmetric (non-anonymous) even with ex-ante symmetric bidders 3. I will give a partial characterization of optimal (potentially asymmetric) mechanisms for n “ 2. An optimal mechanism combines scoring with favoritism in a non-trivial way Relation to literature 1. Procurement with Endogenous Quality (via Scoring Auctions). Che (1993), Asker and Cantillon (2008), Asker and Cantillon (2010), Lewis and Bajari (2011), Decarolis et al.
(2016), . . .
2. Procurement with Exogenous Quality. Manelli and Vincent (1995), Lopomo et al. (2022), . . .
3. Auctions with Investment Before Learning Type. Tan (1992), Piccione and Tan (1996), Arozamena and Cantillon (2004), . . .
4. (Closest.) Auctions with Investment After Learning Type.
Celik et al. (2009), Zhang (2017), Gershkov et al. (2021), . . .
5. (Enormous) literature on contests and tournaments in which all costs are all-pay costs, i.e. Drugov and Ryvkin (2017) In our paper, we blend literatures 1. and 4.

args.summary:
This paper by Andreyanov, Krasikov, and Suzdaltsev (HSE University, 2023) extends the theory of optimal procurement design through scoring auctions when firms face both production costs (incurred only by the winner) and investment costs (incurred by all participants before the auction). While Che (1993) showed that a quasilinear scoring auction is buyer-optimal when only production costs exist, this paper demonstrates that with investment costs, optimal mechanisms are generally asymmetric even with ex-ante symmetric bidders.

Key findings:
1. **Optimal symmetric mechanisms**: When restricted to symmetric mechanisms, the optimal quality schedule q*(θ) decreases with investment costs and the number of bidders (contrasting with Che, 1993, where quality is independent of n). The optimal scoring rule can be implemented via a first-score scoring auction.

2. **Asymmetric mechanisms outperform symmetric ones**: Propositions 5-7 show that for small private information importance (α) or when investment cost elasticity is high relative to the number of bidders, symmetric mechanisms are not optimal. Asymmetry can be optimal even in the limit as n→∞.

3. **Characterization for n=2**: With two bidders, linear production costs (C^P = αθ), and general investment costs (C^I = g(q)), the optimal mechanism depends on the convexity of marginal investment costs:
   - **Sufficiently convex marginal costs**: Optimal mechanism uses score floors (reserve scores), with the favored bidder facing a lower floor and receiving a bonus.
   - **Sufficiently concave marginal costs**: Optimal mechanism uses score ceilings, with the unfavored bidder facing a ceiling and the favored bidder paying a kickback upon winning at the ceiling.

4. **Implementation**: The optimal asymmetric mechanisms can be implemented via modified first-score scoring auctions with discriminatory score floors or ceilings, plus side payments (bonuses or kickbacks) that provide correct incentives to middle types.

5. **Comparative statics**: As the importance of private information (α) grows, optimal mechanisms become more symmetric. The efficient (social planner's) mechanism is more asymmetric than the buyer-optimal mechanism.

6. **Constant-elasticity example**: With C^P = αθ/2, C^I = q^γ/γ, and uniform θ, the optimal mechanism ranges from sole-sourcing to scoring auctions with floors or ceilings, to symmetric mechanisms, depending on parameter values.

The paper concludes that blending investment costs with scoring auctions yields novel optimal mechanisms that combine scoring with favoritism in non-trivial ways.

## Abstract

We prove that, around the symmetric case, where the values are identically distributed, the equilibrium of the first price auction is jointly differentiable with respect to general bidder-specific parameters of the value distributions. We show that the revenue equivalence between the first-price and the second-price auctions to the first-order in the size of the parameters is an immediate consequence of this differentiability and the Revenue Equivalence Theorem; thereby formally establishing the first-order equivalence Fibich et al. [G. Fibich, A. Gavious, A. Sela, Revenue equivalence in asymmetric auctions, J. Econ. Theory 115 (2004) 309-321] noticed for their particular perturbation.

args.summary: This is a RePEc/IDEAS bibliographic entry for the 2009 paper "Auctions with almost homogeneous bidders" by Bernard Lebrun, published in the Journal of Economic Theory (vol. 144(3), pp. 1341-1351). The paper proves that around the symmetric case (where values are identically distributed), the equilibrium of the first-price auction is jointly differentiable with respect to general bidder-specific parameters of the value distributions. The author shows that revenue equivalence between first-price and second-price auctions to the first-order in the size of parameters follows immediately from this differentiability and the Revenue Equivalence Theorem, formally establishing the first-order equivalence that Fibich, Gavious, and Sela (2004) had noticed for their particular perturbation. The paper has 12 references and 6 citations. It is classified under JEL code D44 (Auctions). A working paper version from 2006 is also available.

URL: https://www.weiran-shen.info/page_files/bayesian_nash_equilibrium_in_first-price_auction_with_discrete_value_distributions.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents a study on Bayesian Nash Equilibrium (BNE) in first-price auctions with discrete value distributions. The authors (Zihe Wang, Weiran Shen, and Song Zuo) from Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Carnegie Mellon University, and Google Research provide an algorithm to compute the BNE, prove existence and uniqueness, and characterize the equilibrium structure.

**Key contributions:**
1. An efficient algorithm for computing BNE in first-price auctions under discrete value distributions that does not require solving ordinary differential equations (ODEs), making it faster and more robust than continuous methods.
2. A constructive proof of existence of BNE in the discrete case.
3. A proof of uniqueness of BNE (Theorem 5.4), without requiring the strict log-concavity assumptions needed in continuous cases.
4. Introduction of the "bidding set" concept (Definition 4.1) to analyze how the set of buyers who bid at a given price changes as the bid decreases.
5. The algorithm falls in the "backward-shooting" category—it guesses the largest winning bid and computes strategies down to the smallest winning bid, then iteratively refines the guess.

**Key theoretical results:**
- The smallest winning bid b is determined by the buyer with the largest smallest value (Lemma 2.2).
- Bidding strategies are monotone in value (Lemma 2.5).
- Each buyer's bidding set for a given value is a connected interval (Theorem 4.3).
- The position where the algorithm stops is strictly monotone and continuous in the guessed largest winning bid (Corollary 4.11, Theorem 4.12).

**Experimental results:** The discrete algorithm outperforms continuous approximation methods (e.g., Algorithm 3) in both accuracy and speed. For small instances (n=5, d=5 values), the discrete algorithm finished 955 out of 1000 instances within 30 seconds, while the continuous algorithm finished only 22 instances with tol=0.01. For medium instances (n=10, d=10), the discrete algorithm finished 512 instances while the continuous algorithm finished none.

The paper is motivated by the shift from second-price to first-price auctions in display advertising, where credibility is a major concern. The discrete value setting is justified because real-world observations are finite, and the discrete approach provides structural insights not available in continuous cases.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: Numerical Analysis of Asymmetric First Price Auctions ---
URL: https://capcp.la.psu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/numericalanalysis.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This academic paper (Marshall et al., 1994, Games and Economic Behavior) presents numerical algorithms for solving first-price auction problems where bidders draw independent valuations from heterogeneous (asymmetric) distributions. The heterogeneity analyzed stems from collusion among subsets of bidders.

**Key contributions:**

1. **Problem Context:** Bidders form coalitions that create distributional asymmetries. Two scenarios are examined: (a) two coalitions facing each other, and (b) one coalition facing individual noncooperative bidders.

2. **Numerical Methodology:** The authors develop backward Taylor series expansion algorithms to solve the systems of differential equations characterizing equilibrium bid functions. These are necessary because standard forward methods fail due to pathologies at the origin (nuisance linear solutions acting as attractors). The transformed system (using auxiliary functions δ) proves numerically more stable. Convergence is achieved with N=10,000 subintervals, p=5 order expansions, and error tolerance ε of 10^-5 to 10^-8, requiring about 5 seconds of computation time on a DEC 3100 or 486/33 PC.

3. **Key Results:** 
   - For n=5 bidders, the first-price auction yields higher expected revenue for the seller than the second-price (English) auction when bidder asymmetry arises from collusion.
   - The more optimistic party (larger coalition) shades their bid more.
   - For k1=100, k2=1 (coalition vs individual), the first-price auction generates expected revenue of 0.6578 vs the second-price's 0.4999.
   - Large coalitions (e.g., k1=100) create external benefits for noncolluding bidders at first-price auctions, potentially making large all-inclusive coalitions infeasible.

4. **Theoretical Connections:** The asymmetric distribution problem is equivalent to a first-price auction between bidders with differing degrees of risk aversion. The results are consistent with existence/uniqueness proofs by Lebrun (1991) and Maskin and Riley (1991, 1992).

5. **Implications:** The paper suggests first-price auctions are less susceptible to collusion than second-price auctions, and that small all-inclusive coalitions may be feasible at first-price auctions while large ones may not be. The numerical approach enables investigation of analytically intractable problems and can be extended to more general asymmetric auctions with non-uniform distributions.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: Multiple equilibria in asymmetric first-price auctions ---
URL: https://mpra.ub.uni-muenchen.de/34937/1/MPRA_paper_34937.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This academic paper by Todd R. Kaplan and Shmuel Zamir, published on MPRA in November 2011, challenges the established uniqueness result for Bayes-Nash equilibria in asymmetric first-price auctions. While Maskin and Riley (2003) and Lebrun (2006) proved uniqueness under the assumption that buyers never bid above their values, the authors demonstrate that relaxing this assumption can produce multiple "substantial" additional equilibria. These non-standard equilibria feature buyers who sometimes bid above their values (though never winning with such bids), and can produce different allocations of the object and different selling prices.

The paper uses a detailed example with two buyers (values uniformly drawn from [0,5] and [6,7] respectively) and no minimum bid, showing three distinct equilibria: one standard equilibrium and two non-standard equilibria, each with different revenue outcomes (3.99, 4.27, and 5 respectively) and probabilities of buyer 1 winning (0.133, 0.1, and 0).

The authors prove four key propositions: (1) any standard equilibrium can form a non-standard equilibrium with a smaller minimum bid; (2) if the minimum bid exceeds the maximum possible value, no non-standard equilibrium exists; (3) this condition can be extended to equivalence relationships; and (4) any non-standard equilibrium has an equivalent standard equilibrium with a higher minimum bid. The paper also shows that such multiplicity can only occur in asymmetric auctions—symmetric auctions have no non-standard equilibria. The authors conclude that the assumption that buyers do not bid above their values should be treated more carefully in asymmetric auction analysis.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
